docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: How the four pipeline stages connect to produce a running homelab.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
graph LR
    A[Packer] -->|VM templates| B[Terraform]
    B -->|Provisioned VMs| C[Ansible]
    C -->|Configured hosts| D[Docker]
Stage Tool What It Does 1. Templates Packer Builds cloud-init-enabled Ubuntu images (and a Windows one) on Proxmox 2. Provisioning Terraform Clones templates into VMs with static IPs, CPU, memory, disk 3. Configuration Ansible Installs packages, deploys Docker Compose services, configures networking 4. Runtime Docker Compose Runs all application containers

docs.title: Deployment Order
docs.text:
Infrastructure services have dependencies and must deploy in order:

graph TD
    N[Networking] --> CA[Certificate Authority]
    N --> NTP[Time Server]
    CA --> M[Monitoring]
    NTP --> M
    M --> Apps[Applications]
task ansible:deploy-networking ENV=wil   # 1. DNS, Caddy, Tailscale
task ansible:deploy-ca ENV=wil           # 2. Step-CA
task ansible:deploy-ntp ENV=wil          # 3. Chrony
task ansible:deploy-monitoring ENV=wil   # 4. Prometheus
task ansible:deploy-media ENV=wil        # 5. Applications

Warning

The networking VM must exist before all others — it runs BIND9, which is the nameserver for every other VM.

docs.title: Key Design Decisions
docs.text:
• Docker Compose over Kubernetes — simpler to operate, sufficient for homelab scale
  • Split-horizon DNS with BIND9 — internal clients resolve to internal IPs, external clients to public IP
  • SOPS + Age — secrets encrypted at rest, committed to Git, decrypted at deploy time
  • Caddy — automatic HTTPS with wildcard certificates via Cloudflare DNS-01
  • Task runner — single CLI entry point for all Packer, Terraform, and Ansible operations
  • Data-driven app deployment — most apps share a common deploy-app.yml playbook pattern, configured via apps.yml

docs.title: Environments
docs.text: The homelab supports multiple deployment environments, each with isolated configuration and network ranges.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Environment Purpose Network Range Proxmox Node WIL Development / Primary 10.2.20.0/24 proxmox LDN Production (London) 10.3.20.0/24 pve-lon OVH Dashboard VPS (Virginia), outside the lab none; tailnet name dashboard —

Every task command takes an ENV= variable that threads through to Terraform, Ansible, and Packer:

task ansible:deploy-all ENV=wil
task terraform:deploy ENV=ldn
task packer:build-ubuntu ENV=wil

docs.title: Directory Structure
docs.text:
Terraform and Packer have a directory per environment. Ansible has one inventory for both sites:

AnsibleTerraformPacker 
ansible/inventory/
├── hosts.ini                        # Inventory (both sites)
└── group_vars/
    ├── all/                         # Every host
    │   ├── sites.yml                # One row per site
    │   └── vars.yml                 # Shared variables, services list
    ├── site_wil/                    # wil's own values and secrets
    │   ├── vars.yml                 # site: wil
    │   ├── secrets.sops.yml         # Encrypted secrets
    │   ├── apps.yml                 # wil's app registry
    │   ├── proxy/                   # wil's DNS/proxy entries per domain
    │   ├── infra_networking/        # Networking-specific vars
    │   ├── infra_ca/                # CA-specific vars
    │   └── app_mediastack/          # Media stack vars (wil only)
    └── site_ldn/

terraform/environments/
├── wil/
│   ├── main.tf                      # Calls VM module
│   ├── variables.tf                 # Variable definitions
│   ├── providers.tf                 # Proxmox provider
│   ├── vms.auto.tfvars              # VM definitions
│   └── terraform.tfstate            # State file
└── ldn/

packer/
├── templates/
│   └── ubuntu-server-base.pkr.hcl   # Ubuntu template
└── environments/
    ├── wil/
    │   ├── ubuntu-variables.pkrvars.hcl
    │   └── credentials.wil.pkrvars.hcl.sops  # Encrypted
    └── ldn/

Every host in hosts.ini is listed in its site group ([site_wil], [site_ldn]) and in the role groups the playbooks target, so [infra_networking] lists both .53 VMs. Group variables come from two kinds of folders:

  • all/ — every host. sites.yml has one row per site; domains, system_timezone and the cross-site BIND9 settings (trusted networks, secondary zones, zone transfers, notifies) are derived from it. vars.yml also combines the site's DNS/proxy lists into services.
  • site_<site>/ — that site's own values: its app registry (apps.yml), its DNS/proxy entries (proxy/<domain>.yml), sub-folders named after the group that reads them (they apply to every host of the site), and all of the site's secrets. Groups that run at one site only (app_mediastack, app_frigate, infra_ntp at wil; app_hermes, infra_proxmox at ldn; infra_dashboard, app_kasm_agent at ovh) have their folder there too.
# ansible/inventory/group_vars/all/sites.yml
sites:
  wil:
    cidr: 10.2.0.0/16                   # LAN range
    tz: America/New_York                # Timezone of the site's hosts
    dns: ["10.2.20.53"]                 # BIND9 primary (networking VM)
    ts_router_ips: ["100.103.137.102"]  # Tailnet IP of the subnet router
    zones: [5am.video, 5am.cloud, wil.5am.cloud, ext.5am.cloud, sfc.al]  # Zones it is primary for
  ldn:
    # ...
  ovh:                                  # Dashboard VPS: no LAN or DNS, so no cidr
    tz: America/New_York
    dns: []
    ts_router_ips: []
    zones: []

To add a site, or move a site's DNS server or zones, edit its row, then deploy networking at every site. A site without DNS (ovh) changes nothing at the others.

docs.title: How ENV= Works
docs.text:
ENV names the site and has no default: a task that reads it stops with "Pass ENV=" when it is missing. Terraform and Packer use it to resolve paths; Ansible uses it to limit the run to the site's group: 

# .taskfiles/ansible/Taskfile.yaml
vars:
  HOSTS_FILE: 'inventory/hosts.ini'
  LIMIT: 'site_{{.ENV}}'

# .taskfiles/terraform/Taskfile.yaml
vars:
  ENV_DIR: "environments/{{.ENV}}"

So task ansible:deploy-networking ENV=wil runs ansible-playbook -i inventory/hosts.ini --limit site_wil .... Running ansible-playbook by hand without --limit hits both sites and needs both sites' secrets, which is fine with the master key.

This means the same task commands work across environments — just change ENV=:

task ansible:ping ENV=wil    # Pings WIL hosts
task ansible:ping ENV=ldn    # Pings LDN hosts

docs.title: Shared vs. Environment-Specific Config
docs.text:
Shared across environments:

  • Ansible roles (ansible/roles/)
  • Playbook definitions (ansible/playbooks/)
  • Inventory (hosts.ini) and group_vars/all/ (sites table, derived variables)
  • Terraform modules (terraform/modules/)
  • Packer templates (packer/templates/)

Per-environment:

  • Group variables (group_vars/site_<env>/, including the app registry and proxy lists)
  • VM definitions (vms.auto.tfvars)
  • Secrets (secrets.sops.yml, terraform.tfvars.sops, credentials.*.pkrvars.hcl.sops)
  • Terraform state (terraform.tfstate)

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Wrong environment deployed — Double-check ENV= in your command (there is no default). Run task ansible:ping ENV=<env> to verify you're targeting the right hosts.

Missing environment directory — Each new environment needs a [site_<env>] group in ansible/inventory/hosts.ini, a row in group_vars/all/sites.yml, a group_vars/site_<env>/ folder (with site: <env> in its vars.yml, and an apps.yml, at least apps: {}, which the Taskfile passes to deploy-app and deploy-all), and a terraform/environments/<env>/ directory with the required files.

Cross-site access — WIL and LDN communicate over Tailscale. Ensure the subnet router VM is deployed and advertising routes. See Tailscale.

docs.title: Networking
docs.text:
The homelab runs a unified networking stack across multiple sites: internal DNS, a reverse proxy with automatic TLS, dynamic DNS for external access, and a VPN mesh connecting everything together.

Tip

For deep operational reference, see the Infrastructure Networking docs.

docs.title: Domains
docs.text: Domain Environment Purpose 5am.video WIL Media services (Plex, *arr stack) 5am.cloud WIL Top-level cloud services wil.5am.cloud WIL Internal infrastructure (monitoring, apps) ext.5am.cloud WIL External-facing services sfc.al WIL Personal projects ldn.5am.cloud LDN LDN internal infrastructure

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
graph TD
    subgraph External
        ExtClient[External Client]
        Cloudflare[Cloudflare DNS]
        DDNS[DDNS Updater]
    end

    subgraph Internal
        IntClient[Internal Client]
        BIND9[BIND9 DNS]
        Caddy[Caddy Reverse Proxy]
        Backend[Backend Service]
    end

    IntClient -->|DNS query| BIND9
    BIND9 -->|"proxied service"| Caddy
    BIND9 -->|"direct service"| Backend
    Caddy -->|reverse proxy| Backend

    ExtClient -->|DNS query| Cloudflare
    Cloudflare -->|public IP| Caddy
    DDNS -->|updates IP| Cloudflare
  • Internal clients query BIND9 for service hostnames. Proxied services resolve to Caddy, which terminates TLS and forwards to backends. Non-proxied services resolve directly to the backend.
  • External clients resolve via Cloudflare DNS and reach Caddy over the public IP, kept current by DDNS.
  • Cross-site communication runs over Tailscale WireGuard tunnels. DNS zone transfers replicate zones between sites so each site can resolve the other's services.

docs.title: Key Concepts
docs.text:
• VLANs — each site uses a UDM Pro gateway with VLANs for network segmentation (infrastructure, VMs, storage, clients, IoT). See UniFi Gateway.
  • Split-Horizon DNS — internal and external clients get different answers for the same hostname. See DNS.
  • Unified Service Definitions — a single YAML entry per service drives both DNS records and reverse proxy configuration. See Service Definitions.
  • Zone Transfers — WIL and LDN replicate each other's DNS zones for cross-site resolution. See Zone Transfers.
  • Wildcard TLS — Caddy obtains one wildcard certificate per domain via Cloudflare DNS-01 challenge. See TLS.
  • Static Routes — UDM Pro routes cross-site traffic to the Tailscale subnet router VM. See Static Routes.
  • Port Forwarding — UDM Pro forwards ports 80/443 to Caddy for external access. See Port Forwarding.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Service not resolving internally — Check that BIND9 is running on the networking VM and that the service has an entry in the appropriate domain file under group_vars/site_<env>/proxy/ (or a proxy: block on the app's entry in site_<env>/apps.yml). Redeploy networking: task ansible:deploy-networking ENV=wil.

External access not working — Verify DDNS is updating Cloudflare with the correct public IP. Check that ports 80/443 are forwarded to Caddy on the UDM Pro.

Cross-site resolution failing — Ensure Tailscale is connected on both subnet routers and that zone transfers are configured. Check with dig @10.2.20.53 <hostname>.ldn.5am.cloud.

docs.title: Secrets Management
docs.text: How sensitive configuration is encrypted and managed with SOPS and Age.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Secrets are encrypted at rest with SOPS using Age encryption and committed to Git alongside code. Ansible decrypts them at deploy time via the community.sops collection.

# Edit a secrets file (decrypts in-editor, re-encrypts on save)
sops ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_wil/secrets.sops.yml

# Decrypt to stdout
sops decrypt ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_wil/secrets.sops.yml

# Encrypt a new file
sops encrypt --in-place myfile.yml

docs.title: Age Key
docs.text:
The Age private key lives at ~/.config/sops/age/keys.txt. This key must be present on any machine that needs to decrypt secrets.

# Generate a new key
age-keygen -o ~/.config/sops/age/keys.txt

# View the public key
age-keygen -y ~/.config/sops/age/keys.txt

The public key is configured in .sops.yaml at the repository root.

docs.title: Encrypted File Patterns
docs.text:
SOPS determines which files to encrypt and how based on creation rules in .sops.yaml:

Pattern Encryption Purpose terraform/**/*.tfvars Full file Proxmox credentials, SSH keys packer/**/*.pkrvars.hcl Full file Proxmox API tokens ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_<site>/**/*.sops.yml Full file, master + that site's CI key Ansible secrets (docker\|ansible/(playbooks\|roles))/**/*.sops.yml Full file Docker configs (docker\|ansible)/**/*.env Full file Docker environment files (docker\|ansible/(playbooks\|roles))/**/cf-token Full file Cloudflare API tokens

No rule covers the rest of ansible/inventory/, so sops refuses a secret saved outside a site folder instead of encrypting it for the master key only (which the site's CI could not read).

Tip

Decrypted temporary files match the pattern **/.decrypted~* and are gitignored. Never commit decrypted secrets.

docs.title: Adding a New Secret
docs.text:
1. Every Ansible secret goes in its site's one secrets file, ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_<site>/secrets.sops.yml, so that site's CI key can decrypt it. Open it with sops and add the key under the # --- <group> --- section of the group that reads it (start a section for a new group)
  2. SOPS re-encrypts the file when you save it, for the master key and that site's CI key
  3. Commit the encrypted file
# Add or change a secret
sops ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_wil/secrets.sops.yml

docs.title: Using Secrets in Ansible
docs.text:
Ansible automatically decrypts *.sops.yml files in group_vars/ via the community.sops collection. Reference variables normally:

# In a playbook or template
{{ my_secret_variable }}

docs.title: Terraform and Packer Credentials
docs.text:
The Proxmox tokens live in terraform/environments/<env>/terraform.tfvars.sops and packer/environments/<env>/credentials.<env>.pkrvars.hcl.sops. The Terraform and Packer tasks decrypt them for the one command and pass them as a var file (sops exec-file ... -var-file={}), so nothing is decrypted by hand and no plain-text copy has to stay in the folder.

# Change a value (decrypts in-editor, re-encrypts on save)
sops terraform/environments/wil/terraform.tfvars.sops

# New environment: fill in the example, encrypt it, delete the plain text
cd terraform/environments/<env>
cp ../wil/terraform.tfvars.example terraform.tfvars    # then edit it
sops encrypt terraform.tfvars > terraform.tfvars.sops && rm terraform.tfvars

Packer works the same way, from credentials.<env>.pkrvars.hcl to credentials.<env>.pkrvars.hcl.sops.

docs.title: Rotating the Age Key
docs.text:
1. Generate a new Age key
  2. Update the public key in .sops.yaml
  3. Re-encrypt all files: sops updatekeys <file> for each encrypted file

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
"no matching keys found" — The Age private key at ~/.config/sops/age/keys.txt doesn't match the public key in .sops.yaml. Verify with age-keygen -y and compare.

File not encrypting — Check that the file path matches a creation rule in .sops.yaml. Run sops encrypt explicitly to see the error.

Ansible can't decrypt — Ensure the Age key is present on the machine running Ansible and that community.sops is installed.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
Deploy the homelab from scratch in four steps.

Note

Complete the Prerequisites first. You need Proxmox API tokens, an SSH key, and an Age key before proceeding.

docs.title: 1. Clone and Configure
docs.text:
git clone git@github.com:sfcal/homelab.git
cd homelab

Set your environment once for the shell, or pass ENV= to every task (there is no default):

export ENV=wil

docs.title: 2. Build VM Templates
docs.text:
Build the base Ubuntu template on Proxmox:

task packer:build-ubuntu ENV=wil

This creates a cloud-init-enabled Ubuntu Server template with Docker, Node Exporter, and Lazydocker pre-installed.

docs.title: 3. Provision VMs
docs.text:
Deploy all VMs defined in terraform/environments/wil/vms.auto.tfvars:

task terraform:deploy ENV=wil

To provision a single VM:

task terraform:deploy-vm ENV=wil VM=networking

Warning

The networking VM must be provisioned first — it provides DNS for all other VMs.

docs.title: 4. Deploy Services
docs.text:
Deploy the full infrastructure stack:

task ansible:deploy-all ENV=wil

Or deploy services individually, in dependency order:

task ansible:deploy-networking ENV=wil     # DNS, Caddy, Tailscale
task ansible:deploy-ca ENV=wil             # Step-CA certificate authority
task ansible:deploy-ntp ENV=wil            # Chrony time server
task ansible:deploy-monitoring ENV=wil     # Prometheus
task ansible:deploy-dashboard ENV=ovh      # Grafana, Homepage, Kanidm (OVH VPS)
task ansible:deploy-media ENV=wil          # Plex, *arr stack

docs.title: 5. Verify
docs.text:
# Test connectivity to all hosts
task ansible:ping ENV=wil

# Check a specific service
curl -k https://wil.5am.cloud

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Packer build fails with 401 — Check Proxmox API token credentials in packer/environments/wil/credentials.wil.pkrvars.hcl.sops (open it with sops). Ensure the token has VM.Allocate and Datastore.AllocateSpace permissions.

Terraform can't find template — The template name must match what Packer created. Check with qm list on the Proxmox host. Template names follow the pattern ubuntu-server-<env>-base.

Ansible can't connect — Verify the VM is running (qm status <vmid>), the IP is correct in hosts.ini, and your SSH key is authorized.

DNS not resolving — The networking VM must be deployed first. Other VMs use it as their nameserver (10.2.20.53 in WIL).

docs.title: Add a New VM
docs.text: Provision a new virtual machine on Proxmox using Terraform.

docs.title: 1. Define the VM
docs.text:
Add an entry to terraform/environments/<env>/vms.auto.tfvars:

vms = {
  # ... existing VMs ...

  my_server = {
    name          = "myserver"
    description   = "My new server"
    proxmox_node  = "proxmox"
    vmid          = 1114
    template_name = "ubuntu-server-wil-base"
    ip_address    = "10.2.20.80"
    gateway       = "10.2.20.1"
    nameserver    = "10.2.20.53"
    cores         = 2
    memory        = 4096
    disk_size     = "50G"
    storage_pool  = "local-lvm"
    network_bridge = "vmbr0"
    tags          = "application"
    ssh_user      = "sfcal"
  }
}

Warning

Ensure the vmid and ip_address are unique. Check existing entries in the same file.

docs.title: 2. Provision
docs.text:
Deploy just the new VM:

task terraform:deploy-vm ENV=wil VM=my_server

Or deploy all VMs:

task terraform:deploy ENV=wil

docs.title: 3. Add to Ansible Inventory
docs.text:
Add the VM's IP to ansible/inventory/hosts.ini, in its site group and in the group its playbook targets:

[site_wil]
# ... existing hosts ...
10.2.20.80

[app_myserver]
10.2.20.80

[apps:children]
# ... existing groups ...
app_myserver

docs.title: 4. Verify
docs.text:
# Test SSH access (by IP, or by mDNS name once the clone has booted —
# see docs/infrastructure/networking/unifi.md#mdns for the gateway setting)
ssh sfcal@10.2.20.80
ssh myserver.local

# Test via Ansible
task ansible:ping ENV=wil

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Template not found — The template_name must match exactly one Packer template on the node; otherwise the plan fails at clone.vm_id. Check with qm list on the Proxmox host. Build one with task packer:build-ubuntu ENV=wil.

VMID conflict — Each VM needs a unique VMID. Check existing IDs in vms.auto.tfvars or with qm list.

Can't SSH after provisioning — Cloud-init may still be running. Wait 30 seconds, then retry. Verify the IP is correct and the VM is on the right network bridge.

State conflict — If a VM was deleted by hand, it is still in the Terraform state. Drop it there with terraform state rm 'module.infrastructure.module.vms["<key>"]' in terraform/environments/<env>/, then redeploy. (task terraform:clean only removes the plugin cache.)

docs.title: Certificates
docs.text: The homelab uses two certificate systems: Caddy for public wildcard TLS and Step-CA for private internal certificates.

docs.title: Public TLS (Caddy)
docs.text:
Caddy automatically obtains wildcard certificates for all configured domains using Cloudflare DNS-01 challenges. No manual intervention required.

Any service with proxied: true in its service definition gets automatic HTTPS.

- name: myapp
  backend_host: 10.2.20.60
  backend_port: 8080
  proxied: true  # Automatic TLS via Caddy

Caddy handles certificate issuance, renewal, and OCSP stapling automatically.

docs.title: Private CA (Step-CA)
docs.text: Step-CA provides a private certificate authority for internal services that need TLS but aren't behind Caddy. Both sites chain to one root whose key is on a YubiKey; each site's CA can only issue for its own <site>.5am.cloud names and LAN addresses.

docs.title: Check CA Health
docs.text: task ca:health ENV=wil

docs.title: Fetch the Root Certificate
docs.text:
The root is the same for both sites and is in the repo: ansible/playbooks/infrastructure/ca/files/root_ca.crt. To fetch the copy a CA is serving:

task ca:root ENV=wil

docs.title: Sign a Certificate
docs.text:
task ca:sign ENV=wil CSR=path/to/request.csr

Optionally set a custom duration (default: 8760h / 1 year):

task ca:sign ENV=wil CSR=path/to/request.csr DURATION=2160h

The ca:sign task uploads the CSR to the CA host, signs it with Step-CA, and downloads the signed certificate.

docs.title: When to Use Which
docs.text: Scenario System Why Web app behind Caddy Caddy (automatic) Wildcard cert covers all subdomains Service with self-signed TLS Step-CA Replace self-signed with trusted internal cert Inter-service mTLS Step-CA Issue client and server certificates Backend that Caddy proxies over HTTPS Caddy + tls_skip_verify Or replace backend cert with Step-CA

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Caddy certificate not renewing — Check Caddy logs: ssh <networking-ip> docker logs caddy. Common cause: Cloudflare API token expired or rate-limited by Let's Encrypt. Verify the token in the encrypted secrets file.

Browser shows "not secure" for internal service — The service isn't behind Caddy, or you haven't trusted the Step-CA root certificate. Install the root cert on your device: task ca:root ENV=wil.

Step-CA health check failing — SSH to the CA host and check the container: docker ps, docker logs step-ca. Common cause: the CA container restarted and needs its password file.

docs.title: Deploy a Service
docs.text: Add a new application to the homelab. Most apps use a shared data-driven pattern — define the app in apps.yml and provide a Docker Compose template.

docs.title: Data-Driven Apps (Recommended)
docs.text: Most applications follow this pattern. The shared deploy-app.yml playbook handles everything.

docs.title: 1. Add the App to apps.yml
docs.text:
Add an entry to the registry of the site that hosts the app, ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_<env>/apps.yml:

myapp:
  host_group: app_myapp
  # renovate: datasource=docker
  image: "myimage:latest"
  port: 8080
  proxy:
    name: myapp
    domain: wil.5am.cloud
    proxied: true

There is no images: list — the pre-pull list is derived from every key ending in image. Keep the # renovate: datasource=docker comment directly above the image key and double-quote the value so Renovate can update it. Omit the proxy: block if the app needs no DNS or proxy entry.

docs.title: 2. Create the Compose Template
docs.text:
Create ansible/playbooks/apps/myapp/templates/compose.yaml.j2:

services:
  myapp:
    image: {{ apps.myapp.image }}
    container_name: myapp
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "{{ apps.myapp.port }}:8080"
    environment:
      PUID: "{{ puid }}"
      PGID: "{{ pgid }}"

docs.title: 3. Add to Ansible Inventory
docs.text:
Add a host group to ansible/inventory/hosts.ini, and make sure the host is also listed in its site group:

[site_wil]
# ... existing hosts ...
10.2.20.60

[app_myapp]
10.2.20.60

[apps:children]
# ... existing groups ...
app_myapp

docs.title: 4. Add the Import to site.yml
docs.text:
Add the app to ansible/playbooks/site.yml:

- ansible.builtin.import_playbook: deploy-app.yml
  vars:
    app_name: myapp

docs.title: 5. Task Command
docs.text:
No new task is needed — the shared deploy-app task in .taskfiles/ansible/Taskfile.yaml deploys any registry app by name:

deploy-app:
  desc: "Deploy an app by name (APP=<name>)"
  cmds:
    - task: _deploy
      vars: { PLAYBOOK_PATH: deploy-app.yml, EXTRA_ARGS: '-e app_name={{.APP}} -e @{{.APPS_FILE}}' }

Dedicated tasks (e.g., deploy-media) exist only for apps with custom playbooks.

docs.title: 6. DNS/Proxy Entry
docs.text: The proxy: block from step 1 already covers this — backend_host and backend_port are derived from the app's host_group and port, and the entry is generated when networking is deployed. Manual entries in group_vars/site_<env>/proxy/<domain>.yml are only for services outside the app registry (third-party devices, media stack, monitoring).

docs.title: 7. Deploy
docs.text:
task ansible:deploy-app ENV=wil APP=myapp
task ansible:deploy-networking ENV=wil  # Updates DNS and proxy

docs.title: Custom Playbooks
docs.text:
For apps that need more than Docker Compose (e.g., media stack with NFS mounts), create a full playbook at ansible/playbooks/apps/<service>/deploy.yml:

---
- name: Deploy My Service
  hosts: app_myservice
  become: true

  handlers:
    - name: Include handlers
      ansible.builtin.import_tasks: handlers/main.yml

  pre_tasks:
    - name: Include common prerequisites
      ansible.builtin.include_role:
        name: common

  tasks:
    - name: Deploy service
      ansible.builtin.include_tasks: tasks/deploy.yml

docs.title: If You Need a New VM
docs.text: See Add a New VM first, then come back here after the VM is provisioned.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
App not accessible — Check the app's proxy: block has proxied: true and redeploy networking. Verify the container is running: ssh <host> docker ps.

Container won't start — Check logs: ssh <host> docker logs myapp. Common issues: port conflicts, missing environment variables, image pull failures.

DNS not resolving — Ensure the app has a proxy: block in apps.yml (or, for non-catalog services, an entry in the correct domain file) and redeploy networking: task ansible:deploy-networking ENV=wil.

docs.title: GitOps Deploys
docs.text:
Renovate image bumps deploy themselves. When a Renovate merge to main changes ansible/inventory/group_vars/, the Deploy workflow joins the tailnet from a GitHub-hosted runner and runs the affected playbooks — the same ones task ansible:deploy-* runs — against each environment it touches.

graph LR
    R[Renovate merge] --> P[plan: diff group_vars]
    P --> W[wil: deploy targets]
    W -->|ok| L[ldn: deploy targets]
    W --> TW[move tag deploy/wil]
    L --> TL[move tag deploy/ldn]

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Piece File Trigger, plan, per-environment fan-out .github/workflows/deploy.yml Tailscale, Ansible run, tag marker .github/workflows/deploy-env.yml Changed files → targets .github/scripts/deploy-plan.sh CI deploy user (tailnet-only key) ansible/roles/ci_deploy_user, ansible/playbooks/ci-access.yml Bootstrap tasks .taskfiles/ci/Taskfile.yaml
  • Trigger — push to main touching group_vars, and the head commit is authored by renovate[bot]. Your own commits are never auto-deployed; use task ansible:deploy-* or Run workflow.
  • Plan — diffs group_vars between the environment's tag deploy/<env> (last successful deploy) and the pushed commit. Because the base is the last successful deploy, a run that was cancelled, superseded or failed is picked up by the next one. A changed file counts for an environment when it's in site_<env>/ or in the folder of a group with hosts there; other sites' folders are skipped, and files moved without changes don't count.
  • Targets — only the allowlist below is ever auto-deployed. Anything else that changed is listed in the run summary as "deploy manually".
  • What Renovate merges — image bumps CI can't deploy are never automerged (matchFileNames rule in renovate.json: infra_ca, infra_networking, app_hermes, everything under site_ovh/, and Caddy's Dockerfile.j2). Their PRs stay open until you merge them and deploy by hand, so main never names a version that isn't running. Everything else automerges before 06:00 UTC on weekdays (automergeSchedule), the same window in which Renovate opens PRs, so the deploys land then too.
  • Order — wil first, ldn only if wil didn't fail (no manual approval). One target at a time, and one run at a time: a run waits for the one before it, so it plans from deploy/<env> tags that are up to date. If more runs pile up behind it, GitHub keeps only the newest waiting; that one covers the others' changes, because the plan starts from the last successful deploy.
  • Compose — playbooks apply image bumps with compose up (state: present), which recreates only the services whose image or definition changed.
  • Note — a playbook always deploys the whole current state of main for its stack. Anything you pushed but didn't deploy for that stack goes out too.

docs.title: Auto-deploy allowlist
docs.text:
Changed under group_vars/ Runs site_<env>/apps.yml deploy-app.yml for each app whose entry changed site_<env>/app_mediastack/ apps/media/deploy.yml site_<env>/app_frigate/ apps/frigate/deploy.yml site_<env>/app_gaming/ apps/gaming/deploy.yml site_<env>/infra_monitoring/ infrastructure/monitoring/deploy.yml site_<env>/infra_netboot/ infrastructure/netboot/deploy.yml

Never auto-deployed: infra_ca, infra_networking, infra_ntp, infra_proxmox, all/, site_<env>/proxy/, and other files directly in site_<env>/. CI has no SSH access to those hosts at all. app_hermes isn't on the allowlist either: deploy it by hand (see Hermes Agent). To change the allowlist, edit PLAYBOOK_FOR in deploy-plan.sh and the host pattern in playbooks/ci-access.yml (task ci:known-hosts reads its hosts from that playbook). A group that pins an image and stays off the allowlist also belongs in the no-automerge rule in renovate.json.

docs.title: Security model
docs.text:
• The runner joins as an ephemeral tag:ci node using workload identity federation — no long-lived Tailscale secret.
  • The Tailscale policy grants tag:ci TCP 22 to the deploy hosts only. ldn-gateway also advertises the Haivision corporate /16s, so the grant must stay host-specific.
  • CI logs in as deploy, whose key carries from="<site gateway LAN IP>". The subnet router SNATs tailnet traffic, so the key only works when it arrives via the tailnet. deploy has passwordless sudo (every play uses become), so treat SSH_DEPLOY_KEY as root on the deploy hosts.
  • Each environment has its own CI age key. .sops.yaml encrypts ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_<env>/**/*.sops.yml to master + that CI key only, so CI can't read Terraform/Packer credentials or the other environment's secrets. That's why every Ansible secret lives in its site's folder, and why each job runs with --limit site_<env>: without it the run would need the other site's secrets too.
  • Secrets are GitHub environment secrets (wil, ldn), so they're only released to jobs running in that environment.
  • Logs — the workflow never runs with --diff or -v; rendered templates contain decrypted secrets.

docs.title: One-time setup
docs.text: Do wil first; ldn is the same with ENV=ldn.

docs.title: 1. Tailscale
docs.text:
Grants are additive and "src": ["*"] matches tagged devices, so the default allow-all has to be replaced, not added to. autogroup:member excludes tagged devices, and the subnet CIDRs keep site-to-site traffic working (* used to cover traffic from approved subnets: zone transfers, cross-site services, wil → Haivision via ldn-gateway). In the policy file:

"tagOwners": {
  "tag:ci": ["autogroup:admin"],
},

"hosts": {
  // CI deploy targets (keep in sync with ansible/playbooks/ci-access.yml)
  "wil-media":      "10.2.0.5",   // media stack + frigate
  "wil-monitoring": "10.2.20.30",
  "ldn-monitoring": "10.3.20.30",
  "ldn-work":       "10.3.20.50",
  "ldn-gaming":     "10.3.20.55",
  "ldn-netboot":    "10.3.20.60",
  "ldn-kosync":     "10.3.20.70",
  // used by tests only
  "wil-ns":      "10.2.20.53",
  "ldn-ns":      "10.3.20.53",
  "wil-ca":      "10.2.20.9",
  "ldn-pve":     "10.3.20.10",
  "corp-sample": "10.5.0.1",
},

"grants": [
  // Your devices: everything, as before.
  {"src": ["autogroup:member"], "dst": ["*"], "ip": ["*"]},
  // Site-to-site: hosts behind either subnet router.
  {"src": ["10.2.0.0/16", "10.3.0.0/16"], "dst": ["*"], "ip": ["*"]},
  // CI deploy runners: SSH to deploy targets only.
  {
    "src": ["tag:ci"],
    "dst": [
      "wil-media", "wil-monitoring",
      "ldn-monitoring", "ldn-work", "ldn-gaming", "ldn-netboot", "ldn-kosync",
    ],
    "ip": ["tcp:22"],
  },
],

"tests": [
  {
    "src": "tag:ci",
    "accept": ["wil-media:22", "ldn-work:22"],
    "deny": ["wil-media:32400", "wil-ns:22", "wil-ca:22", "ldn-pve:8006", "corp-sample:22"],
  },
  {"src": "sfcal@github", "accept": ["wil-ns:22", "ldn-pve:8006", "corp-sample:443"]},
  {"src": "wil-ns", "accept": ["ldn-ns:53"]},
  {"src": "ldn-ns", "accept": ["wil-ns:53"]},
],

Connections initiated from the Haivision ranges into the homelab are no longer allowed (replies to your own connections still are); add those /16s to the site-to-site src if anything there dials in.

Then create a federated identity for GitHub Actions with:

  • subject repo:sfcal/homelab:environment:wil (one identity per environment)
  • the writable auth_keys scope, restricted to tag:ci

Note the client ID and audience. With Tailnet Lock enabled, federation won't work: you'd need a pre-signed ephemeral auth key and the action's statedir instead.

docs.title: 2. Keys, deploy user, host keys
docs.text:
From your machine, on the LAN or tailnet:

task ci:keys ENV=wil               # CI SSH + age keys in ~/.config/homelab-ci/wil, re-encrypts wil secrets
task ansible:deploy-ci-access ENV=wil
task ci:known-hosts ENV=wil        # writes ansible/inventory/known_hosts/wil
git add .sops.yaml ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_wil ansible/inventory/known_hosts/wil && git commit -m "ci deploy keys for wil"

docs.title: 3. GitHub
docs.text:
task ci:secrets ENV=wil            # creates the environment, sets SSH_DEPLOY_KEY + SOPS_AGE_KEY
gh secret set TS_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID --env wil
gh secret set TS_AUDIENCE --env wil

Optional variables (repo- or environment-level):

Variable Purpose DEPLOY_ENVS Environments Renovate merges auto-deploy to. Default wil; set wil ldn to enable prod TS_PING A tailnet peer (e.g. wil-gateway's 100.x address) the action pings before deploying DEPLOY_NOTIFY_URL ntfy-style URL; receives a POST per target with the result

docs.title: 4. Test
docs.text: Actions → Deploy → Run workflow, env wil, target playbook:infrastructure/monitoring/deploy.yml. Once that's green, Renovate merges deploy wil on their own.

docs.title: 5. Enable ldn
docs.text:
Repeat steps 2–3 with ENV=ldn (federated identity subject repo:sfcal/homelab:environment:ldn), test with app:kosync, then set DEPLOY_ENVS to wil ldn. ldn then deploys unattended once wil has succeeded — no approval step.

Images that only exist in ldn (kosync, the work apps, RomM, Wolf) have no wil canary; Renovate's minimumReleaseAge (1 day minor, 3 days major) is their buffer. If you ever want a pause before prod without having to approve anything, give the ldn environment a wait timer (free on public repos) — the run waits, and you can cancel it in that window.

docs.title: Day to day
docs.text:
• Manual deploy — Run workflow with app:<name> or playbook:<path>. With an empty target, it deploys everything changed since deploy/<env> and moves the tag.
  • Rollback — git revert the Renovate commit. The revert is yours, not Renovate's, so deploy it with Run workflow (empty target) or task ansible:deploy-*.
  • Skipped changes — the run summary lists files that changed but aren't auto-deployed.
  • :latest images — Renovate opens no PRs for floating tags (pinDigests: false), so they never trigger a deploy. Pin a real tag to bring an image under GitOps.

docs.title: Networking Changes
docs.text: Common DNS, proxy, and routing operations.

docs.title: Add a Service to DNS and Proxy
Registry apps
docs.text:
For apps in the app registry, add a proxy: block to the app's entry in its site's registry, ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_<env>/apps.yml. Use a zone of that site: a site's networking reads only its own registry.

# site_wil/apps.yml
myapp:
  host_group: app_myapp
  # renovate: datasource=docker
  image: "myimage:latest"
  port: 8080
  proxy:
    name: myapp
    domain: wil.5am.cloud
    proxied: true

Then redeploy networking:

task ansible:deploy-networking ENV=wil

backend_host and backend_port are derived automatically: the first inventory host of the app's host_group, and the app's port (override with backend_port inside the proxy: block).

docs.title: Non-catalog services
docs.text:
For services outside the registry (third-party devices, media stack, monitoring), add an entry to the domain's file in the proxy folder of the site that is primary for it, ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_<env>/proxy/:

# wil.5am.cloud.yml
- name: myapp
  backend_host: 10.2.20.60
  backend_port: 8080
  proxied: true

Then redeploy networking as above.

Either path creates both a DNS A record (myapp.wil.5am.cloud → Caddy) and a Caddy reverse proxy entry.

Tip

Set proxied: false if the service handles its own TLS or doesn't need a reverse proxy. The DNS record will point directly to backend_host.

docs.title: Service Definition Options
docs.text:
Field Required Default Description name yes — Subdomain (e.g., myapp → myapp.wil.5am.cloud) backend_host yes — Backend IP address backend_port yes — Backend port proxied yes — true for Caddy proxy, false for direct DNS enabled no true Set false to disable both DNS and proxy dns no — Set external to skip internal A record tls_skip_verify no false Backend uses self-signed HTTPS forward_headers no false Adds X-Real-IP, X-Forwarded-For host_header no — Overrides Host header to upstream encode no — Response encoding (e.g., gzip) read_buffer no — Read buffer size auth no false Require a Kanidm login

For registry-generated entries, backend_host and backend_port are derived — the proxy: block only supplies name, domain, proxied, and any optional fields.

docs.title: Add a New Domain
docs.text:
1. Create a domain file in the proxy folder of the site that will be primary for it, ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_<env>/proxy/:

    # mydomain.com.yml
mydomain_services:
  - name: app1
    backend_host: 10.2.20.60
    backend_port: 8080
    proxied: true

  2. Add the domain to the site's zones in group_vars/all/sites.yml:

    sites:
  wil:
    # ...
    zones: [5am.video, 5am.cloud, wil.5am.cloud, ext.5am.cloud, sfc.al, mydomain.com]

  3. Add the list to the services aggregation in group_vars/all/vars.yml:

    services: >-
  {{
    (
      ...
      (mydomain_services | default([]) | map('combine', {'domain': 'mydomain.com'}) | list) +
      registry_services
    ) | selectattr('domain', 'in', sites[site].zones) | list
  }}

  4. Redeploy networking at every site, so the other sites pick up the new zone as secondaries: task ansible:deploy-networking ENV=wil, then ENV=ldn

docs.title: Add a PTR Record
docs.text:
PTR records (reverse DNS) are not generated from the services list — the reverse zone template (reverse.zone.j2) is rendered from the dns_ptr_records list in group_vars/site_<env>/infra_networking/bind9.yml. Add an entry there for any host that needs reverse DNS.

See DNS — Reverse DNS for details.

docs.title: Set Up Cross-Site Zone Transfer
docs.text:
Zone transfers between sites (e.g., WIL ↔ LDN) are derived from group_vars/all/sites.yml: every site's BIND9 is a secondary for the other sites' zones. To change them:

  1. Edit the site's row in group_vars/all/sites.yml (dns, ts_router_ips, zones)
  2. Redeploy networking at every site
  3. Ensure Tailscale connectivity between sites

See DNS — Cross-Site Zone Transfers for the full configuration.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
DNS not resolving after change — Redeploy networking: task ansible:deploy-networking ENV=wil. Check BIND9 logs: ssh <networking-ip> docker logs bind9.

Certificate not issued — Caddy uses DNS-01 via Cloudflare. Verify the Cloudflare API token is valid and the domain's nameservers point to Cloudflare. Check Caddy logs: ssh <networking-ip> docker logs caddy.

Zone transfer failing — Verify Tailscale connectivity between sites. Check that allow-transfer includes the remote site's DNS server IP. Test with dig AXFR <zone> @<primary-dns>.

docs.title: Provision a CM5 over the Network
docs.text: Netboot-provision (or re-image) a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5 time-server node to a fresh Ubuntu install on its eMMC. Covered nodes and their identities live in cm5_hosts in ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_ldn/infra_netboot/vars.yml (currently CM1, 10.3.30.11 and CM2, 10.3.30.12).

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
The Pi EEPROM bootloader is not UEFI — it never runs netboot.xyz or iPXE, and Ubuntu for Pi ships as a preinstalled image, not an installer. The netboot VM (10.3.20.60) therefore serves a parallel Pi boot tree next to the existing x86 flow:

graph LR
    CM5["CM5
(VLAN 30)"] -->|"TFTP: <short-serial>/config.txt
kernel + initramfs + dtb"| NB["netboot VM
10.3.20.60"]
    CM5 -->|"HTTP :8080
modloop / apkovl / img.xz / seed"| NB
  1. The bootloader TFTP-fetches boot files from a directory named after the last 8 hex digits of the module serial (89c03c1a/ for CM1). Other VLAN 30 clients are unaffected — the Pi ignores the UniFi boot filename option, and x86 clients never request Pi paths.
  2. It boots a tiny Alpine Linux flasher (kernel + initramfs over TFTP; module image and flash script over HTTP).
  3. The flasher streams ubuntu-26.04-preinstalled-server-arm64+raspi.img.xz from the netboot VM straight onto /dev/mmcblk0, then writes the node's cloud-init seed (hostname, static IP, SSH keys) onto the system-boot FAT partition, and reboots into the fresh OS.

Always armed, by design. The per-serial payload is permanently served, but BOOT_ORDER=0xf2461 tries eMMC → NVMe → USB → network, so a healthy node never netboots. Only a blank or unbootable module falls through — and then it provisions itself, zero-touch. The trade-off is deliberate: an eMMC that stops booting gets reflashed, not debugged. To exempt one node without removing its payload, drop a file named disabled in /srv/netbootxyz/assets/cm5/<full-serial>/ on the netboot VM.

Interrupted flashes are safe. The flasher zeroes the partition table first and writes it back last, so a power cut mid-flash always leaves the eMMC non-bootable — the boot loop re-enters the flasher and retries.

docs.title: One-time EEPROM prerequisites (per CM5)
docs.text:
The Pi bootloader is not reliably served by the UDM's DHCP boot option, so the TFTP server is pinned in EEPROM. On the node (or via the ptp-experiments EEPROM provisioning):

sudo rpi-eeprom-config --edit

Add alongside the existing BOOT_ORDER:

TFTP_IP=10.3.20.60
TFTP_FILE_TIMEOUT=60000
BOOT_WATCHDOG_TIMEOUT=300

Keep NETWORK (nibble 2) in BOOT_ORDER — it is the terminal fallback this whole flow depends on. Verify after reboot with vcgencmd bootloader_config.

docs.title: Provision a blank module
docs.text:
Nothing to do: publish its identity and deploy, then plug it in. It falls through to network boot and flashes itself.

  1. Add the module to cm5_hosts (full 16-hex serial from cat /proc/device-tree/serial-number, or the sticker) with hostname/IP/gateway/nameserver.
  2. task ansible:deploy-netboot ENV=ldn (first run downloads the ~90 MB Alpine tarball and ~1.4 GB Ubuntu image onto the netboot VM).
  3. Power the module on VLAN 30. Flash takes roughly 5–10 minutes; it comes up on its static IP with SSH keys installed.

docs.title: Re-image a working node (manual, deliberate)
docs.text:
A healthy node never netboots on its own. Trigger it from the node — preferred (one-shot, auto-clearing, falls back to the old OS if the flasher fails to load):

ssh sfcal@10.3.30.11 'sudo vcmailbox 0x0003808b 4 4 0xf12 && sudo reboot'

0xf12 = try NETWORK first, then eMMC, this boot only (set_reboot_order, EEPROM ≥ 2025-01-14). Fallback for older firmware — on Pi 5-family, config.txt presence is the bootability test:

ssh sfcal@10.3.30.11 'sudo mv /boot/firmware/config.txt /boot/firmware/config.txt.disarmed && sudo reboot'

(The flasher restores a fresh config.txt by reflashing; there is no undo short of moving the file back before rebooting.)

After the reflash, re-run the ptp-experiments Ansible — the flash resets the tryboot A/B state (autoboot.txt, current/, new/) to the stock single-boot layout.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Module loops without flashing — tcpdump -i any port 69 on the netboot VM; expect a request for <short-serial>/config.txt. No request: check TFTP_IP in EEPROM (vcgencmd bootloader_config) and that the NIC is the built-in ethernet (the bootloader netboots only on that). Request for the wrong dir: cm5_hosts serial doesn't match — the TFTP dir is the last 8 hex digits.
  • Alpine boots but nothing happens — check http://10.3.20.60:8080/cm5/<full-serial>/apkovl.tar.gz and user-data return 200, and that no disabled file exists for the serial. Console messages are prefixed cm5-flash:.
  • Flash is slow — TFTP (kernel+initramfs, ~28 MB) is lockstep and slow by protocol; the big transfers ride HTTP. Total ~5–10 min is normal.
  • Ubuntu image URL 404s — point releases displace the filename on cdimage.ubuntu.com (26.04.1 ~Aug 2026); bump cm5_ubuntu_image_url/cm5_ubuntu_image_sha256, or fetch the GA image from old-releases.ubuntu.com. The cached copy on the netboot VM keeps working regardless.
  • Never place a config.txt or pieeprom.* at the TFTP root (/var/lib/netbootxyz/config/menus/) — the former would hijack every Pi on the VLAN, the latter would trigger silent EEPROM self-update on netbooting Pis.

docs.title: Re-image the Time Server
docs.text:
Reset the PTP time server (LattePanda MU, timeserver, 10.3.30.123, LDN VLAN 30) to a fresh Ubuntu install over the network. The loop is: PXE boot the MU → wait for the unattended install → the MU reboots into fresh Ubuntu → re-run the ptp-experiments Ansible. There is no confirmation prompt anywhere in that loop.

The MU is a physical UEFI x86 SBC managed by the separate ptp-experiments repo — the homelab provides only the netboot service that lays down the base OS. (The Raspberry Pi CM5 time-server nodes use a different mechanism on the same netboot VM — see Provision a CM5.)

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
graph LR
    MU["LattePanda MU
(VLAN 30)"] -->|"DHCP + PXE"| UDM["UDM Pro
Network Boot option"]
    UDM -->|"TFTP: netboot.xyz.efi"| NB["netboot VM
10.3.20.60"]
    MU -->|"HTTP :8080
kernel / initrd / ISO / seed"| NB

The UDM Pro's VLAN 30 DHCP scope points PXE clients at the netboot VM running netboot.xyz (see UniFi Gateway — Network Boot).

The netboot.xyz bootloader chains MAC-${mac:hexhyp}.ipxe from the TFTP root before falling back to menu.ipxe, so a per-MAC script scoped to the MU's PXE NIC boots it straight into the installer with no menu interaction — every other VLAN 30 client still gets the standard menu. That script passes autoinstall on the kernel line, so the install runs start to finish with no prompts — reaching it is the re-image.

The per-MAC script is always staged — there is no arm/disarm step, mirroring the CM5 flasher. A healthy node boots from its local disk and never reaches PXE; it lands in the installer only when local boot fails or PXE is deliberately chosen from the firmware boot menu. When the install finishes the node reboots straight into the fresh OS (a node that still cannot boot locally just re-enters the unattended install — a re-image loop until local boot succeeds).

A PXE boot of a listed MAC wipes the disk

The installer loads immediately and runs unattended — no ESC/countdown, no disk-wipe confirmation. The only way to abort is to power the MU off before it partitions. Every other VLAN 30 client still gets the standard netboot.xyz menu, which times out to local disk in ~10s.

docs.title: The timecard blacklist
docs.text: The MU's timecard runs PTM-enabled firmware that hangs the box the moment the in-tree ptp_ocp binds, so timeserver_blacklist_modules blocks it in both places a hang can happen: module_blacklist= on the iPXE kernel line (installer environment) and /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-timecard.conf, written by an autoinstall late-command and baked into the initramfs (installed system). The ptp-experiments driver playbook lifts the block once it has built a compatible module.

docs.title: Pre-flight
docs.text:
1. Verify the Ubuntu release on the MU. The DKMS drivers in ptp-experiments (igc-ppsfix, ptp-ocp-gnsspps) are built against the MU's current kernel series, so the re-install must use the same release:

    ssh sfcal@10.3.30.123 'lsb_release -sr; uname -r'

    (10.3.30.123 is the address the entry pins on re-image; an MU that predates the pin answers on its older address. Console fallback if SSH is down.)

  2. Pin the release in ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_ldn/infra_netboot/vars.yml: set netboot_ubuntu_iso_url and netboot_ubuntu_iso_sha256 (from the SHA256SUMS file next to the ISO; superseded interim releases move to old-releases.ubuntu.com — point the URL there for the exact base image). Then redeploy:

    task ansible:deploy-netboot ENV=ldn

    The first run downloads the ~3 GB ISO onto the netboot VM.

  3. Confirm the PXE MAC. Each time server is an entry in timeserver_hosts in the netboot vars, keyed by its PXE NIC's MAC (lowercase, --separated). Check the MU's key matches the NIC that PXE-boots — on the MU, ip -br addr shows the NIC holding 10.3.30.123 (currently enp1s0, 40:a6:b7:81:7c:51: the address iPXE presented in the netboot VM's nginx log on 2026-08-28 and 2026-10-13, not the ethtool -P one), converting : separators to -. The installed OS pins the entry's ip statically via this MAC, so the address is deterministic and no longer depends on the UniFi DHCP reservation — though keeping the reservation as a backstop does no harm.

    After a NIC swap

    The MAC keys three things: the MAC-<mac>.ipxe boot hook, the HTTP seed directory, and the installed system's netplan match (which is why a swapped NIC comes up with no network — collect the new MAC at the console, not over SSH). Update the timeserver_hosts key and redeploy; the play sweeps the old hook and seed dir on its own. Read the MAC with sudo ethtool -P enp1s0 rather than ip -br link — iPXE presents the burned-in address, so a software MAC override would make the hook silently miss.

  4. Nothing to back up — the grandmaster's state is fully rebuilt by ptp-experiments. Note that Grafana/Prometheus history under /opt/monitoring on the MU is lost on re-image.

docs.title: Re-image
docs.text:
1. PXE boot the MU: reboot it and pick the network boot entry from the firmware boot menu. (A broken MU that cannot boot its disk lands there on its own — that is the self-provisioning path.)
  2. The installer loads and starts immediately — no ESC/countdown, no confirmation. To abort, power off before it partitions the disk.
  3. Wait for the unattended install to finish. The MU reboots into the fresh install off local disk — coming up as sfcal with SSH keys installed and the static address 10.3.30.123.

docs.title: Restore
docs.text:
From the ptp-experiments repo:

ansible-playbook -i hosts.ini deploy.yml -l ptp_server

The two DKMS drivers only load after a reboot (the playbook flags /run/reboot-required rather than rebooting) — reboot when prompted and re-run if needed.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• iPXE times out fetching the boot file — check the VLAN 30 Network Boot option and that UDP 69 / TCP 8080 reach 10.3.20.60 (see the firewall notes in the UniFi doc).
  • Installer ignores the seed / runs fully interactive — first check the nginx access log on the netboot VM for a second full-ISO fetch with user-agent Cloud-Init: cloud-init treats casper's url= kernel argument as a cloud-config URL and re-downloads the whole ISO into RAM before reading the seed. The cloud-config-url=/dev/null argument in timeserver-reimage.ipxe.j2 suppresses this — if it's missing, that's the cause. Otherwise verify http://10.3.20.60:8080/timeserver/<mac>/user-data, meta-data, network-config, and vendor-data all return 200 (the <mac> directory is the host's timeserver_hosts key), and diagnose from the installer console: Ctrl+Alt+F2, then cloud-init status --long, ls /autoinstall.yaml, and dmesg | grep -i oom. Any edit to timeserver-reimage.ipxe.j2 deploys on the next task ansible:deploy-netboot ENV=ldn run.
  • MU drops to the netboot.xyz menu instead of the installer — its timeserver_hosts key does not match the NIC that actually PXE-booted, or the netboot service has not been redeployed since the entry was added. Confirm the file exists as MAC-<mac>.ipxe in /var/lib/netbootxyz/config/menus/ on the netboot VM. After a NIC swap, also check the firmware's network-boot entry still points at the NIC whose MAC is in timeserver_hosts — a second onboard NIC has no boot hook and falls through to the menu.
  • Re-imaged MU comes up on the wrong IP — the installed OS pins the entry's ip (10.3.30.123) by the PXE NIC's MAC. If it lands elsewhere, the booting NIC's MAC does not match the host's timeserver_hosts key.
  • Kernel boots then stalls loading the ISO — the url= boot loads the whole ISO into RAM; the client needs more RAM than the ISO size. wget: short write: No space left on device at ~96% (seen 2026-10-13) is the initramfs root tmpfs, capped at half of RAM; rootfstype=ramfs on the kernel line (in timeserver-reimage.ipxe.j2) lifts the cap so only total RAM limits it.

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text:
Deep operational reference for each infrastructure service. Deploy in dependency order.

task ansible:deploy-proxmox ENV=ldn      # 0. Hypervisor (SR-IOV GPU VFs), ldn only; needs root SSH to the PVE host
task ansible:deploy-networking ENV=wil   # 1. Must be first
task ansible:deploy-ca ENV=wil           # 2. Certificate authority
task ansible:deploy-ntp ENV=wil          # 3. Time server
task ansible:deploy-monitoring ENV=wil   # 4. Metrics and dashboards

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
1. Proxmox Hosts — SR-IOV GPU virtual functions and PCI resource mappings on the hypervisor
  2. Networking — DNS (BIND9), reverse proxy (Caddy), dynamic DNS, VPN (Tailscale)
  3. Certificate Authority — Private CA (Step-CA) for internal TLS
  4. Time Server — NTP synchronization (Chrony)
  5. Monitoring — Metrics (Prometheus), dashboards (Grafana and Homepage, on the OVH VPS), uptime (Uptime Kuma)
  6. Docker Services — Container definitions and compose templates
  7. Gaming — Wolf (Moonlight streaming) and RomM on the GPU VM (ldn)
  8. Hermes Agent — AI agent on the Claude subscription (ldn)

docs.title: Docker Services
docs.text: All homelab services run as Docker Compose stacks deployed by Ansible. The docker_service role handles directory creation, compose template rendering, image pulling, and container lifecycle.

docs.title: Media Stack
docs.text:
The media stack provides automated media management and streaming on a dedicated host (app_mediastack):

Service Purpose Plex Media streaming server Sonarr TV show management Radarr Movie management Prowlarr Indexer management Sabnzbd Download client Bazarr Subtitle management Tdarr Media transcoding Pulsarr Request management Frigate Camera/NVR integration

Deploy with task ansible:deploy-media ENV=wil.

docs.title: Gaming
docs.text: Wolf and RomM (ldn) share one playbook on the app_gaming host; an environment gets the stacks its group_vars define. Deploy with task ansible:deploy-gaming ENV=<env>; see Gaming.

docs.title: Hermes Agent
docs.text: Hermes Agent (ldn) has its own playbook, which also installs Claude Code and the Claude subscription plugin in the container. Deploy with task ansible:deploy-hermes ENV=ldn; see Hermes Agent.

docs.title: Kasm
docs.text:
Kasm (ldn, on the work VM, https://kasm.ldn.5am.cloud) is the LinuxServer image, which runs Kasm's own Docker daemon inside the container. Its state is under /var/lib/kasm/. Deploy with task ansible:deploy-kasm ENV=ldn.

Custom workspace images live in ansible/playbooks/apps/kasm/files/, one folder per image with a Dockerfile (folder names lowercase: they become the image name). Each image is built on one machine only, the one whose agent runs its workspace, listed in kasm_workspace_images:

Machine List Built by Agent work VM site_ldn/app_kasm/vars.yml (none now) task ansible:deploy-kasm ENV=ldn, inside Kasm's Docker 85a6c3 OVH VPS site_ovh/app_kasm_agent/vars.yml (deluge) task ansible:deploy-kasm-agent ENV=ovh, in the VPS's Docker (Kasm Agent) a67ee6

Each deploy copies the build files over and builds localhost/<folder>:latest, pulling newer base images first. To use one, add a workspace with that image name and restrict it to that machine's agent: the other agent doesn't have the image. To move one, move its name to the other list, change the workspace's agent, then deploy the machine that now builds it. Agents prune images in Aggressive mode: within 30 s they delete any image no workspace of theirs uses, so save the workspace first, then deploy.

docs.title: Deluge
docs.text:
The Deluge workspace runs localhost/deluge:latest (files/deluge/) on the OVH VPS agent, so torrent traffic leaves from the VPS's IP, with no volume mappings. When a torrent finishes, Deluge's Execute plugin runs torrent-archive, which writes it as one uncompressed <torrent name>.zip into ~/Downloads, so Kasm's download panel can fetch it in one go (written as .zip.part first, then renamed; zip -0, since media doesn't compress). Torrents download to ~/torrents. Both folders, and Deluge's settings, last only as long as the session: fetch the archives before ending it. The settings come from the image (core.conf, execute.conf), which Kasm copies into each new session's home; mapping ~/.config to a host folder would overwrite what's saved there each time. The base stays on the Kasm server's version. Deluge 2.0.3 with libtorrent 2.0 logs a harmless KeyError: 'disk.num_blocks_cache_hits' every few seconds.

Workspace settings (Kasm's admin, not this repo): Docker Image localhost/deluge:latest, Docker Registry empty, Restrict Image to Kasm Agent a67ee6 (the VPS), Volume Mappings {}.

docs.title: Data-Driven Apps
docs.text:
Most applications use the shared deploy-app.yml playbook and are defined in the registry of the site that hosts them, ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_<env>/apps.yml. See Deploy a Service for the full workflow.

App Image Port Ignis (Obsidian) nobbe/ignis 8082 iSponsorBlockTV ghcr.io/dmunozv04/isponsorblocktv — KOReader Sync koreader/kosync 17200 MicroBin danielszabo99/microbin 8081 Restreamer datarhei/restreamer 8710

docs.title: Ignis
docs.text: Ignis (ldn, on the work VM) runs Obsidian in the browser at https://ignis.ldn.5am.cloud, behind the Kanidm login: it has no login of its own. Everything it keeps is on the VM's own disk under /var/lib/work/ignis/: vaults/ (one folder per vault, plain Markdown), data/ (Ignis settings and sync state) and obsidian-app/ (the Obsidian download, fetched again when missing). A rebuilt VM starts with no vaults.

docs.title: iSponsorBlockTV
docs.text:
iSponsorBlockTV (ldn, on the web VM) skips SponsorBlock segments and ads on YouTube TV apps. It has no web UI and only needs to reach youtube.com, so it has no port or proxy entry. Paired TVs and settings are in /var/lib/isponsorblocktv/data/config.json on the VM, written by the setup wizard, not by Ansible; a rebuilt VM needs its TVs paired again. Until a TV is paired the container exits every 10 seconds and restarts.

To pair a TV (also to add another one or change settings), open YouTube on the TV, go to Settings → Link with TV code, then on the VM:

cd /opt/isponsorblocktv
docker compose run --rm isponsorblocktv setup      # setup-cli for plain prompts
docker compose restart

docs.title: Infrastructure Services
docs.text:
Infrastructure services have dedicated playbooks rather than using the data-driven pattern:

Service Docs BIND9, Caddy, oauth2-proxy, DDNS, Tailscale Networking Prometheus, Grafana, Homepage Monitoring (Grafana and Homepage on the OVH VPS) Step-CA Certificate Authority

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Compose templates — Jinja2 templates at ansible/playbooks/apps/<service>/templates/compose.yaml.j2
  2. Rendering — Ansible renders templates with environment-specific variables from group_vars/
  3. Deployment — The docker_service role creates the service directory, renders the compose file, pulls images, and starts containers
  4. Restart policy — All containers use unless-stopped
  5. LinuxServer images — Use PUID, PGID, UMASK environment variables for file permissions

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Container not starting — Check logs: ssh <host> docker logs <container>. Common issues: port conflicts, missing environment variables, image not found.

Image pull failed — Verify network connectivity on the host. For GHCR images, ensure no rate limiting. Retry with ssh <host> docker pull <image>.

Compose file not updating — Ansible only re-renders the template when variables change. Force a redeploy by modifying a variable or deleting the deployed compose file on the host.

docs.title: Gaming (Wolf, RomM)
docs.text:
One playbook, ansible/playbooks/apps/gaming/deploy.yml, deploys every game stack on an environment's app_gaming host. A stack runs only where that environment's group_vars/site_<env>/app_gaming/vars.yml defines its image (romm_image, wolf_image). Both run at ldn:

Environment VM Stacks ldn gaming (10.3.20.55, VM 3005) Wolf and RomM 
task ansible:deploy-gaming ENV=ldn   # Wolf and RomM

To run a stack in another environment, copy its vars into that environment's group_vars/site_<env>/app_gaming/vars.yml, along with its secrets.

docs.title: Files
docs.text: Path Purpose ansible/playbooks/apps/gaming/deploy.yml Playbook (group app_gaming) ansible/playbooks/apps/gaming/templates/wolf-compose.yaml.j2 Wolf container (matches the upstream quickstart compose) ansible/playbooks/apps/gaming/templates/wolf-config.toml.j2 Wolf config.toml (version 7), seeded once ansible/playbooks/apps/gaming/templates/romm-compose.yaml.j2 RomM and MariaDB ansible/playbooks/apps/gaming/templates/romm-config.yml.j2 RomM library layout ansible/playbooks/apps/gaming/files/85-wolf.rules Upstream udev rules (/dev/uinput, /dev/uhid, virtual pads off the host seat) ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_ldn/app_gaming/vars.yml Wolf and RomM images, paths, render node ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_ldn/secrets.sops.yml RomM database, auth and IGDB secrets (section app_gaming)

docs.title: Wolf and RomM
docs.text:
Wolf streams games and desktops to Moonlight clients from the gaming VM (ldn, 10.3.20.55, VM 3005) using an Intel Arc Pro B50 SR-IOV virtual function. RomM manages the ROM library the Wolf emulator apps read.

Prerequisite: the VF must be visible in the guest, which depends on the Proxmox host play. The playbook aborts if the render node (wolf_render_node, /dev/dri/renderD128) is missing.

The play ends with docker compose up -d for both stacks. Compose recreates a container whenever its stored config hash differs from the current one, which ends any Moonlight session and restarts MariaDB, even when compose.yaml did not change (seen 2026-10-18). Before deploying while someone is streaming, compare the hashes on the VM; identical hashes mean no recreate:

ssh sfcal@10.3.20.55 'for p in wolf romm; do docker compose --project-directory /opt/$p config --hash="*"; done; docker inspect wolf romm romm-db --format "{{.Name}} {{index .Config.Labels \"com.docker.compose.config-hash\"}}"'

docs.title: How Wolf is deployed
docs.text:
• Wolf runs as root in one container with the Docker socket, /dev and /run/udev mounted; it starts the app containers (Wolf UI, Pegasus, RetroArch, Steam) as siblings and maps paths back to the host by introspecting its own container. No host paths are passed in.
  • State lives in /var/lib/wolf/state on the VM, mounted at /etc/wolf. Wolf reads /etc/wolf/cfg/config.toml, keeps TLS keys next to it and per-app data under profile-data/<profile>/<runner name>/ (for example profile-data/user/WolfPegasus), which each app sees as /home/retro.
  • config.toml is seeded on the first deploy only (force: false). Wolf rewrites the file when a client pairs and when apps or profiles change through Wolf UI or its API, so re-rendering it would drop pairings. To add or change an app on a running host, see Changing apps on a running Wolf.
  • The seed contains the default Moonlight profile (Wolf UI, a synthetic "Test ball" stream useful to check the encoder) and a User profile with Pegasus, RetroArch (both with ROMs at /ROMs) and Steam, plus the upstream [gstreamer] encoder table. On Intel, Wolf picks the first working VA-API encoder.
  • No memory limit is set on the Wolf container: the app containers are siblings, so a limit would only starve the compositor and encoder.
  • Steam Input does not work inside the Steam container (known Wolf limitation, issues #81 and #403): it hides the Wolf pad from games and replaces it with a virtual gamepad created through uinput, whose device node never appears inside the container because no udev runs there. Do not pass /dev/uinput to the Steam app; that only makes Steam stop its keyboard/mouse fallback, which breaks menus and look. Disable Steam Input per game (Properties > Controller) and let the game read the "Wolf X-Box One (virtual) pad" directly. Symptom of Steam Input being on: look and jump work (emulated mouse/keys) but analog movement does not.
  • Games never see the physical controller. Moonlight sends a controller type (Xbox, PS, Nintendo, Steam or unknown) plus capability flags, and Wolf creates a matching virtual pad on the VM: "Wolf X-Box One (virtual) pad" for Xbox and unknown, "Wolf DualSense (virtual) pad" for PS, "Wolf Nintendo (virtual) pad" for Nintendo. Wolf (revision facb8e0) does not know the Steam type that moonlight-qt sends for a Steam Controller since August 2026, so it falls into the unknown branch: a client that also advertises gyro or accelerometer gets a DualSense pad, otherwise an Xbox pad. The game-side binds (Half-Life autoexec.cfg) are verified against the Xbox pad only. To keep that pad for a motion-capable controller such as the Steam Controller (2026), pin it per client in /var/lib/wolf/state/cfg/config.toml and restart Wolf between sessions: 
    [[paired_clients]]
app_state_folder = '...'
client_cert = '''...'''
[paired_clients.settings]
motion_controller_override = "XBOX"   # or controllers_override = ["XBOX"] to force slot 0 regardless of motion
    Precedence is controllers_override (per slot) over motion_controller_override over auto-detection. The Steam Controller's trackpads, gyro and grip buttons only reach a game through Steam Input, which cannot run inside the Wolf Steam container, so with the Xbox pad it behaves as a plain Xbox-layout pad. Without Steam running on the client the controller only acts as a gamepad where the client's SDL is new enough (moonlight-qt nightly/Flatpak with SDL 3.4.10 or later); on Android TV and Apple TV it appears as a keyboard and mouse (the d-pad types arrow keys, so Half-Life "moves on the d-pad" and Wolf never logs a joypad).

docs.title: Changing apps on a running Wolf
docs.text:
Wolf owns config.toml after the first seed, so editing wolf-config.toml.j2 only affects future re-seeds. To apply an app change to the running host without re-pairing:

  1. Render the template locally or deploy (the play never overwrites the live file) and copy the new [[profiles.apps]] block.
  2. Append it to /var/lib/wolf/state/cfg/config.toml under the [[profiles]] it belongs to (the user profile is last in the file, so appending at the end adds to it). Check the result parses: python3 -c 'import tomllib; tomllib.load(open("/var/lib/wolf/state/cfg/config.toml","rb"))'.
  3. docker restart wolf when no session is streaming. Wolf reads the file only at start-up; paired_clients are kept.

Wolf's API (unix socket wolf.sock inside the Wolf container's /run/user/wolf volume) is not a shortcut here: POST /api/v1/apps/add only adds to the Moonlight profile, apps added through the API cannot stream until the next restart anyway (upstream PR #506), and any API-driven profile write drops the Test ball [profiles.apps.video]/[profiles.apps.audio] overrides from the file.

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
Moonlight talks directly to the VM; it cannot go through Caddy. Ports: 47984/tcp, 47989/tcp, 47999/udp, 48010/tcp, 48100/udp, 48200/udp. wolf.ldn.5am.cloud is a plain A record for the VM. Pair a client by opening the PIN URL Wolf logs (http://wolf.ldn.5am.cloud:47989/pin/#<secret>).

RomM is proxied as https://roms.ldn.5am.cloud (container port 8080, host port 8085).

docs.title: ROM library
docs.text:
romm_library_path (/srv/romm/library) holds roms/<platform>/<game> and bios/<platform>, RomM's default layout. Pegasus and RetroArch mount roms/ at /ROMs. The library is local to the VM; to use a NAS, set gaming_nfs: true in ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_ldn/app_gaming/vars.yml, put the mount in nfs_mounts in ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_ldn/nfs.yml and point romm_library_path at the mount.

GameCube games go in roms/gc/ and Wii games in roms/wii/ (the play creates both). RomM maps gc to its ngc platform, and these are the folder names the Pegasus image scans; roms/ngc/ would work for RomM but not Pegasus.

Back up /var/lib/romm/db and /var/lib/romm/assets (saves and states); resources is a regenerable metadata cache.

docs.title: Verify in the guest
docs.text:
ssh sfcal@10.3.20.55
lspci -nn | grep -i display                      # Intel Battlemage G21 [8086:e212]
sudo dmesg | grep -iE 'xe .*SR-IOV|PRELOADED'    # Running in SR-IOV VF mode
ls -l /dev/dri                                   # renderD128
docker logs wolf 2>&1 | grep -iE 'encoder|vendor|pin'

A successful qm start is not yet a successful stream: Linux-guest 3D on Battlemage VFs is still maturing upstream. Use the "Test ball" app to confirm encoding before debugging a game.

docs.title: Hermes Agent
docs.text:
Hermes Agent runs on its own VM in ldn, hermes (10.3.20.80, VM 3008), from the official Docker image. It uses your Claude subscription through Nous Research's Claude Subscription DirectSDK plugin, which runs the official Claude Code CLI, so it needs no API key.

task terraform:deploy-vm ENV=ldn VM=hermes_server   # The VM
task ansible:deploy-hermes ENV=ldn                  # Hermes, Claude Code and the plugin

docs.title: Sign in to Claude
docs.text:
Do this once, by hand. Open the URL it prints, sign in and paste the code back:

ssh sfcal@10.3.20.80
docker exec -it -u hermes hermes claude auth login

The login stays in the data directory, so it survives redeploys and new images. Keep -u hermes: without it the command runs as root and saves the login where Hermes doesn't look.

docs.title: Use
docs.text:
docker exec -it hermes hermes                 # Chat
docker exec -it hermes hermes model           # Change the model (the first deploy sets Opus 5.5)
docker exec -it hermes hermes gateway setup   # Connect Telegram, Discord and so on

No ports are published, so there is no web UI and no DNS or Caddy entry. The agent's terminal and file tools run inside the container as UID 10000, with no access to the Docker socket.

docs.title: Telegram
docs.text:
Hermes polls Telegram, so this opens no ports. Create a bot with @BotFather (/newbot) and get your numeric user ID from @userinfobot. Then run the wizard on the VM, choose Telegram and Manual, and enter the token and your ID when asked. Only the IDs you list can use the bot.

docker exec -it hermes hermes gateway setup
docker restart hermes

Always run the docker restart afterwards: in this container the wizard's own restart only stops the gateway, and Telegram stays disconnected until the container restarts.

The token stays in /var/lib/hermes/data/.env on the VM, not in the repo, so a rebuilt VM needs this again. The wizard's Automatic option is less work, but the token then comes through a service Nous Research hosts.

docs.title: Fix Plex problems
docs.text:
Text the bot about something on Plex, such as a failed download, bad sound or the wrong HDR format. The plex-fix skill checks the file and how Plex is playing it, suggests a replacement and asks before grabbing it. The old file stays until the new one imports, and Hermes checks back about 30 minutes later. /plex-fix also starts it.

Hermes reaches Radarr, Sonarr and Plex on 10.2.0.5 over the site tunnel, using the keys in group_vars/site_ldn/secrets.sops.yml (section app_hermes). These are copies of the keys Homepage uses in wil, so update both if you rotate one.

  • Format preference: SDR or HDR10 first, and no Dolby Vision-only files. Change this in SKILL.md.
  • Limits: Hermes can't hear or see a file, so sound fixes are best guesses. If a replacement ranks lower than the current file, Radarr or Sonarr refuses the import and the old file stays. Hermes can't finish a manual import either.
  • Safety: the keys can delete anything. An approvals.deny rule blocks DELETE calls to the media server from the terminal, but it's a seat belt rather than a hard limit.
  • Recycle bin: Radarr and Sonarr move replaced files to /data/recycle/<app> on the NAS and remove them after 7 days. This is set in each app under Settings > Media Management, not in this repo.

docs.title: Sort email
docs.text:
The fastmail-triage skill sorts what the Fastmail sieve leaves in the Inbox into Receipts, Finance, Subscriptions, Notifications and Newsletters. It runs on Mondays. At 08:00 London time a model with no tools classifies senders and subject lines, and at 08:30 a script checks those answers, moves the mail and sends a report to Telegram. Message bodies are never read.

A deploy installs the skill and both jobs. Create the token by hand, once: in Fastmail, go to Settings > Privacy & Security > Connected apps & API tokens > Manage API tokens, and make a JMAP token with only Email ticked. Then paste it at the hidden prompt:

ssh -t sfcal@10.3.20.80 docker exec -it -u hermes hermes python3 /opt/data/skills/email/fastmail-triage/scripts/fastmail_triage.py set-token

The token stays on the VM, not in the repo, so a rebuilt VM needs this again. Keep -u hermes, or Hermes can't read the file.

A new install only reports what it would move. Check the setup, try a run, and turn on moving when the report looks right:

ssh sfcal@10.3.20.80
docker exec -u hermes hermes python3 /opt/data/skills/email/fastmail-triage/scripts/fastmail_triage.py check
docker exec -u hermes hermes hermes cron run fastmail-triage-decide
docker exec -u hermes hermes hermes cron run fastmail-triage-apply
docker exec -u hermes hermes python3 /opt/data/skills/email/fastmail-triage/scripts/fastmail_triage.py mode apply

After that, text the bot to sort now, show the last report, undo a sort, or always file a sender somewhere.

  • What it can do: move mail out of the Inbox into those five folders, up to 150 messages a run and 40 per sender. Every move can be undone. It holds back people, conversations, flagged mail and subjects about payments, security and other matters on its protected lists.
  • Personal settings: your addresses, protected senders and the phrases that say something about your life are in hermes_fastmail_site_config in group_vars/site_ldn/secrets.sops.yml (section app_hermes), because this repo is public. Keep them out of default-config.json. The scan refuses to run if they're missing.
  • Safety: mail text only reaches a model with no tools, so a hostile subject line has nothing to act with. Reports carry counts and short sender addresses, never subject lines. Fastmail's Email scope can also delete mail, and the agent's terminal could read the token file, so don't ask Hermes to read mail text in chat.
  • History: Hermes saves each job's prompt, and a chat search can find it. The 08:30 job deletes those prompts, and the report says if that fails, so subject lines are searchable for about 30 minutes each week.

The design notes are in references/design.md, and python3 -I ansible/playbooks/apps/hermes/tests/test_fastmail_triage.py runs the offline tests.

docs.title: Usage limits
docs.text:
Hermes draws from your subscription's usage limits, the same limits as your other Claude use. Turn off extra usage in your Claude account if you don't want overage billing.

Nous Research labels the plugin experimental. Hermes' built-in anthropic provider isn't used because its Claude sign-in only spends extra-usage credits on a Max plan.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text:
Run task ansible:deploy-hermes ENV=ldn to update everything:

  • Hermes — Renovate bumps hermes_image, but app_hermes isn't on the auto-deploy allowlist, so the VM doesn't change until you deploy.
  • Skills — each deploy copies the repo's skills over the VM's. Hermes can edit its own skills as it learns, and a deploy overwrites those edits, so copy any you want to keep into the repo first. docker exec hermes hermes curator ledger lists them, and earlier versions are in /var/lib/hermes/data/.curator_backups/blobs. fastmail-triage is locked, so Hermes can't edit it.
  • Claude Code and the plugin — each deploy moves both to their current release. They live in the data directory, so a new image keeps them. Claude Code doesn't update itself here, because the plugin turns that off.
