docs.title: Kasm Agent (OVH VPS)
docs.text:
ldn's Kasm (the LinuxServer image on the work VM, 10.3.20.50) has a second Docker agent on the OVH VPS (site ovh, 135.148.219.216, tailnet 100.116.40.99). It runs the Deluge workspace, so its torrent traffic leaves from the VPS's IP, with the custom image localhost/deluge:latest built on the VPS (Docker Services → Kasm). Deluge ran on the work VM for part of 2026-11-09 and came back the same day.

task ansible:deploy-kasm-agent ENV=ovh

The playbook (playbooks/apps/kasm-agent/) installs the official Kasm 1.18.1 agent, the same version as the work VM's Kasm, with its release checked against a pinned sha256. It runs the installer once, and Kasm's own upgrade.sh handles later versions. It also:

  • creates a 2 GB swap file (/mnt/Kasm.swap), which the installer asks for;
  • installs kasm-agent-guard, an nftables table that drops the agent's port (4443) on the public interface before Docker's port forwarding sees it, so only the tailnet reaches the agent;
  • builds the custom workspace images named in kasm_workspace_images (now deluge) from playbooks/apps/kasm/files/ in the VPS's Docker, with build files copied to /opt/kasm-agent/images/;
  • creates Deluge's folders under /var/lib/kasm-agent/deluge/ (used by the old stock-image setup; the custom image maps nothing).

Values: group_vars/site_ovh/app_kasm_agent/vars.yml. The manager token is in the app_kasm_agent section of site_ovh/secrets.sops.yml (a copy of the token the work VM's own agent uses).

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
• Agent → Kasm: 10.3.20.50:4443 over the tailnet (the VPS accepts ldn's subnet route).
  • Kasm → agent: 100.116.40.99:4443. The ldn UDM has a static route for 100.116.40.99/32 via ldn-gateway (10.3.20.53); without it, sessions don't start.
  • One port for both: the installer uses its --proxy-port both for the agent's own port and for reaching Kasm, so the agent uses Kasm's port, 4443.

docs.title: Settings in Kasm's admin (not in this repo)
docs.text: Where Setting Why Infrastructure → Docker Agents 100.116.40.99 enabled The VPS agent Infrastructure → Deployment Zones → default Upstream Auth Address 10.3.20.50 (was proxy) Each agent's proxy checks the login at this address. proxy only resolves inside the work VM's Kasm; on the VPS it is the agent's own proxy, so sessions there failed with a 404 on /api/internal_auth/ Workspaces → FileZilla, Tor-Browser Restrict Image to Kasm Agent: 85a6c3 (the work VM) Keeps them off the VPS. A new agent pulls the image of every unrestricted workspace, so restrict any new container workspace too Access Management → Groups → All Users → Settings keepalive_expiration 604800 (was 3600) See Sessions below Workspaces → Deluge Docker Image localhost/deluge:latest, Docker Registry empty, Restrict Image to Kasm Agent a67ee6, Volume Mappings {} The custom image, built on the VPS by this playbook Workspaces → Deluge (stock image, until 2026-11-09) Restrict Image to Kasm Agent a67ee6, Memory 2048 MB, Volume Mappings /var/lib/kasm-agent/deluge/downloads → /home/kasm-user/Downloads and /var/lib/kasm-agent/deluge/config → /home/kasm-user/.config (uid/gid 1000) How Deluge ran on the VPS. Map all of ~/.config, not ~/.config/deluge: Docker would create ~/.config as root, and the image's startup script then fails copying its default profile there (the container exits at once). Not for the custom image, which keeps its settings in the image

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
Deluge only downloads while its session exists. Kasm deletes a session keepalive_expiration seconds after its browser tab last sent a keepalive (keepalive_expiration_action: delete). Group All Users has it at 604800 (one week), raised from 3600 on 2026-11-07 so Deluge keeps downloading with the tab closed. Kasm group settings can't be limited to one workspace, so every session of the group lasts that long; your account falls back to All Users because Administrators sets nothing here. A session picks up a new value at its next keepalive, which reopening it sends.

With the custom image, an expired Deluge session takes its torrents and archives with it (nothing is mapped to the host). They live in the session container's own layer on the VPS's root disk (75 GiB since 2026-11-09), and each finished torrent takes about twice its size until the session ends: the torrent and its zip.

docs.title: Proxmox Hosts (SR-IOV GPU)
docs.text:
The hypervisor is managed by ansible/playbooks/infrastructure/proxmox/deploy.yml, group infra_proxmox. Its one job: create the Intel Arc Pro B50's SR-IOV virtual functions (VFs) at every boot, before Proxmox starts the VMs that use them.

task ansible:deploy-proxmox ENV=ldn

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A GPU VM references its VF through a resource mapping (hostpci0: mapping=b50-vf1, pci_mapping in Terraform). At VM start Proxmox resolves the mapping against sysfs and refuses to start if the device is missing or its IOMMU group changed:

PCI device mapping invalid (hardware probably changed): pci device '0000:0b:00.1' not found

VFs exist only after something writes to sriov_numvfs, and they vanish on reboot.

docs.title: What the play installs
docs.text:
Path on pve-ldn Purpose /usr/local/sbin/sriov-b50 Finds the PF by PCI id (lspci -d 8086:e212), waits for the xe driver, writes sriov_numvfs, binds the VFs to vfio-pci /etc/systemd/system/sriov-b50.service Oneshot, Before=pve-guests.service, runs the script

Then it runs pvesh get /cluster/mapping/pci --check-node pve-ldn, the same validation qm start performs, and fails if a mapping no longer matches the hardware.

Configuration (ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_ldn/infra_proxmox/vars.yml):

b50_num_vfs: 3

The card itself (PCI id 8086:e212, unit and mapping names) is hardcoded in the play and templates.

docs.title: Facts worth knowing
docs.text:
• Kernel 7.0 (Proxmox VE 9.2) supports Battlemage SR-IOV out of the box: no module option, DKMS or force_probe. 6.17 (PVE 9.1) did too; 7.0 adds per-VF debugfs quotas (/sys/kernel/debug/dri/<PF>/sriov/vfN/tile0/vram_quota) for an uneven VRAM split, unused here.
  • The card's firmware data (igsc fw-data version -d /dev/mei0) sets sriov_totalvfs: Intel's current image (203.41) allows 2 VFs, the launch image (203.31, from driver package 32.0.101.6979, flashed on 2026-11-03) allows 12. Each VF's BAR is 16 GB divided by the VF count, rounded up to a power of two (8 GB with 2 or 3 VFs, 4 GB with 4), and the VRAM is split evenly between the VFs (about 5.2 GiB each with 3).
  • Mapping IDs are b50-vf1 (VM 3005 gaming), b50-vf2 (VM 121 ubuntu-desktop-kasmvnc, moved from VM 3004 work on 2026-11-05) and b50-vf3 (VM 118 windows-gpu). They are created once in Datacenter > Resource Mappings, or with pvesh create /cluster/mapping/pci --id b50-vfN --map node=pve-ldn,path=<VF address>,id=8086:e212,subsystem-id=8086:1114,iommugroup=<group>. If a kernel or BIOS change moves a VF's IOMMU group, the play fails and names the mapping; fix it in Datacenter > Resource Mappings.
  • Never add options vfio-pci ids=8086:e212 or blacklist xe: vfio-pci would claim the physical function and no VF could exist.
  • To change b50_num_vfs, edit the variable, re-run the play, and reboot the host: the count can only change while no VM holds a VF. With the GPU VMs stopped, systemctl restart sriov-b50 does the same without a reboot.
  • Never run an Intel Windows installer against the bare PF, and never fwupdmgr update on the host: both re-flash the 2-VF firmware data. Guests holding a VF cannot flash anything. Both config-data images are kept in /root on pve-ldn (b50fw-6979 is the 12-VF one, b50fw the 2-VF rollback).
  • A guest needs kernel 6.17 or newer for a Battlemage VF (Ubuntu 25.10 qualifies; Ubuntu 24.04 needs linux-generic-hwe-24.04, its 6.8 kernel has no driver for the card). VFs are render-only, no display outputs.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
ssh root@10.3.20.10 'systemctl status sriov-b50; lspci -nnks 0b:00; pvesh get /cluster/mapping/pci --check-node pve-ldn'

Expect 0b:00.0 on xe, 0b:00.1 to 0b:00.3 on vfio-pci, and no checks on the mappings. After a reboot qm status 3005 should be running without manual action.

docs.title: Terraform notes
docs.text:
The GPU VM game_server is defined in terraform/environments/ldn/vms.auto.tfvars with bios = "ovmf", machine = "q35" and pci_mapping. work_server keeps bios and machine but no longer maps a VF; VMs 118 and 121 are hand-made clones outside Terraform, given their VF with qm set <vmid> --hostpci0 mapping=b50-vfN,pcie=1. The provider is bpg/proxmox (proxmox_virtual_environment_vm). The module sets rombar = true on the mapped device because bpg sends rombar=0 when it is left out. On apply the provider also starts a stopped VM (started defaults to true), so a stopped GPU VM is started and needs its VF free.

Since November 2026 the ldn state holds all eight ldn VMs as proxmox_virtual_environment_vm (imported when the provider changed from telmate), and the wil state holds wil's three (networking, ca_server, monitoring_server; wil's node is named proxmox). A VM made outside Terraform is imported with <node>/<vmid> as the ID. The import needs the site's variables, decrypted for the one command the way the tasks do it:

cd terraform/environments/ldn
sops exec-file --filename terraform.tfvars terraform.tfvars.sops \
  'terraform import -var-file={} "module.infrastructure.module.vms[\"<key>\"].proxmox_virtual_environment_vm.vm" pve-ldn/<vmid>'

Then read the plan from the repo root: task terraform:plan ENV=ldn. An import changes only the state file, never the VM.

The VM module ignores clone changes so an imported VM does not plan as a replacement, and changes to the login keys (ssh_public_key): on an existing VM the provider would rewrite the cloud-init drive and reboot the VM, which then sets itself up as a new instance (new SSH host keys). wil's three VMs were made with one key and have the second in authorized_keys. Always read the plan before applying (task terraform:deploy ENV=ldn applies with -auto-approve): anything marked forces replacement would destroy the VM.

docs.title: Certificate Authority (Step-CA)
docs.text:
Step-CA provides a private certificate authority for issuing internal TLS certificates. It runs as a Docker container on a dedicated VM in each environment, enabling services to communicate over HTTPS without relying on public CAs.

Deployment order

Step-CA deploys after Networking and before NTP, monitoring, and applications.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
graph TD
    Root[5am Root CA<br/>key on the YubiKey]
    WIL[WIL intermediate<br/>wil.5am.cloud, 10.2.0.0/16]
    LDN[LDN intermediate<br/>ldn.5am.cloud, 10.3.0.0/16]
    Service1[Services at wil]
    Service2[Services at ldn]

    Root -->|signs| WIL
    Root -->|signs| LDN
    WIL -->|issues certs| Service1
    LDN -->|issues certs| Service2

There is one root for both sites. Its key was generated on a YubiKey (PIV slot 9c) and cannot be copied off it; every signature needs the PIN and a touch. There is no backup: if the YubiKey is lost, the intermediates keep working until they expire, but a new root has to be made and trusted everywhere.

Each site's Step-CA holds an intermediate signed by that root. The intermediate carries name constraints, so it can only issue for its own site's domain (<site>.5am.cloud and anything under it), its LAN range and 127.0.0.1. Step-CA refuses other names, and clients reject such a certificate even if one were made with a stolen intermediate key. Services request certificates via the ACME protocol or the step CLI. Devices only need to trust the one root, ansible/playbooks/infrastructure/ca/files/root_ca.crt.

docs.title: Root and intermediates
docs.text:
Needs ykman, step and the step-kms-plugin on the machine with the YubiKey.

# Once, ever: change the PIN and PUK, then make the root on the YubiKey
ykman piv access change-pin
ykman piv access change-puk
task ca:root-init

# Per site, and again before an intermediate expires (5 years)
task ca:sign-intermediate ENV=wil
task ansible:deploy-ca ENV=wil

ca:sign-intermediate makes a new intermediate key on the site's CA (it never leaves the VM), signs it on the YubiKey and saves the certificate as files/intermediate_ca_<site>.crt. The deploy installs the root and the intermediate, switches to the new key only if it matches the certificate, deletes the key of the root Step-CA made for itself on first start, and restarts the CA. A site with no signed intermediate in files/ keeps Step-CA's self-made chain.

task ansible:deploy-ca ENV=wil

The task file performs these steps in order:

  1. Creates /opt/step-ca/ (compose, password file) and /var/lib/step-ca/data/ (CA state)
  2. Deploys the provisioner password file (mode 0600)
  3. Deploys compose.yaml from template
  4. Starts the Step-CA container
  5. Waits 10 seconds for initialization
  6. Runs a health check against https://127.0.0.1:9000/health
  7. Sets the certificate duration claims and the ACME provisioner in ca.json via jq (rewritten, and the CA restarted, only when a value differs)
  8. Exports the root CA certificate to /opt/step-ca/root_ca.crt
  9. Displays status output

Source: ansible/playbooks/infrastructure/ca/tasks/step-ca.yml

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text:
The container runs smallstep/step-ca with the following configuration:

  • Port: 9000 (HTTPS API)
  • Volumes: ./data for CA state, ./password.txt mounted read-only
  • Restart policy: unless-stopped
  • Initialization: handled via DOCKER_STEPCA_INIT_* environment variables on first run

docs.text:
task ca:health ENV=wil

Or manually:

curl -k https://ca.wil.5am.cloud:9000/health

docs.title: Export the root CA certificate
docs.text:
The root certificate is automatically exported during deployment to /opt/step-ca/root_ca.crt. To retrieve it:

ssh sfcal@10.2.20.9 cat /opt/step-ca/root_ca.crt

docs.title: Change certificate duration
docs.text:
1. Edit ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_<env>/infra_ca/vars.yml:

    step_ca_default_cert_duration: "2160h"   # 90 days
step_ca_max_cert_duration: "17520h"      # 2 years

  2. Deploy:

    task ansible:deploy-ca ENV=wil

The task compares ca.json with these values on each run. It rewrites the file and restarts the CA only when they differ, so a deploy that changes nothing leaves the CA running.

docs.title: Restart the CA
docs.text:
The playbook handlers support lifecycle management:

# Full redeploy (will restart automatically if config changes)
task ansible:deploy-ca ENV=wil

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
The monitoring stack provides metrics collection, visualization, a service dashboard, and external uptime monitoring. Prometheus runs as a Docker container on a dedicated VM in each environment; Grafana, Homepage and Uptime Kuma run once for both sites on an OVH VPS outside the lab (see Grafana and Homepage).

Deployment order

Monitoring deploys after Networking, Step-CA, and NTP. It is the last infrastructure service to deploy before applications.

docs.text:
The task file:

  1. Creates the directory structure: rendered config under /opt/monitoring/, Prometheus state under /var/lib/monitoring/
  2. Sets ownership to monitoring_uid:monitoring_gid
  3. Deploys Prometheus configuration
  4. Deploys Docker Compose file
  5. Starts all containers and removes any that are no longer in compose.yaml

docs.title: Prometheus
docs.text: Prometheus scrapes metrics from node exporters running on infrastructure and application VMs.

docs.title: Scrape Configuration
docs.text:
The prometheus.yml.j2 template generates the scrape config:

global:
  scrape_interval: 15s
  evaluation_interval: 15s

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'prometheus'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['localhost:9090']

  - job_name: 'node-exporter'
    static_configs:
      - targets:
          - 'localhost:9100'
          - '10.2.0.5:9100'
          # ... all node targets

Three additional jobs — chrony, gpsd, and node — scrape the PTP grandmaster's exporters (deployed by the ptp-experiments repo's monitoring role). Each renders only when its per-environment target list is non-empty; currently only LDN defines them. The node job is kept separate from node-exporter because the Chrony dashboard's CPU-temperature panel selects job="node" unscoped.

docs.title: Container Configuration
docs.text:
• Memory: 2GB limit, 1GB reservation
  • Retention: configurable via prometheus_retention
  • Storage: persistent volume at /prometheus
  • User: runs as monitoring_uid:monitoring_gid

Source: ansible/playbooks/infrastructure/monitoring/templates/prometheus.yml.j2

docs.title: Grafana
docs.text: One Grafana covers both sites. It runs on the OVH VPS next to Homepage, in the same compose project (/opt/dashboard, state in /var/lib/dashboard/grafana), and reads each site's Prometheus over the tailnet, so it stays up when a site is down; that site's graphs are then empty.

docs.title: Access
docs.text: Tailnet only: http://dashboard:3000. Grafana listens on 127.0.0.1:3000, and tailscale serve puts it on the tailnet's port 3000. Anyone on the tailnet can view the dashboards without signing in; sign in as admin to edit. There is no grafana.<site>.5am.cloud name any more.

docs.title: Datasource Provisioning
docs.text:
files/grafana/provisioning/datasources/datasources.yml provisions one Prometheus datasource per site:

Name uid URL Prometheus (wil) prometheus-wil (default) http://10.2.20.30:9090 Prometheus (ldn) prometheus-ldn http://10.3.20.30:9090

The uids are fixed because the provisioned dashboards bind to them. Grafana reads datasources at start; the playbook restarts it when the file changes.

docs.title: Dashboard Provisioning
docs.text:
Dashboards are provisioned from files — any JSON dropped into playbooks/infrastructure/dashboard/files/grafana/dashboards/ is deployed and picked up automatically (the file provider rescans every 30 s; UI edits to provisioned dashboards do not persist):

Dashboard File Data Chrony Detail chrony_grafana_dashboard.json chrony + node jobs (PTP grandmaster), from prometheus-ldn GPSD gpsd_grafana_dashboard.json gpsd job (PTP grandmaster), from prometheus-ldn Node Exporter Full node_exporter_full.json All node-exporter/node targets, site picked with the Datasource variable (grafana.com 1860) System Activity system_activity.json CPU, memory, network and disk I/O per node-exporter target, site picked with the Site variable (?var-ds=prometheus-wil or prometheus-ldn); Homepage embeds its four panels

A new dashboard either binds to one site's uid or gets a datasource variable (type datasource, query prometheus) and uses ${<variable>} as each panel's datasource uid.

docs.text:
• Memory: 1GB limit, 256MB reservation
  • Ports: 127.0.0.1:3000 only
  • Provisioning: mounted read-only at /etc/grafana/provisioning
  • Sign-up: disabled (GF_USERS_ALLOW_SIGN_UP=false)
  • Embedding: allowed, and anyone who is not signed in gets read-only access (GF_SECURITY_ALLOW_EMBEDDING, GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_*), so Homepage can show panels in iframes without a Grafana login

docs.title: Homepage
docs.text: Homepage provides a service dashboard with status widgets, service health indicators, and quick links to all homelab services. One instance covers both sites and runs on an OVH VPS (135.148.219.216, Virginia), so it stays up when a site is down; its cards then show what is unreachable.

docs.title: Access
docs.text:
Tailnet only: http://dashboard/ (needs Tailscale's DNS on the device, which adds the tailnet's search domain). Homepage listens on 127.0.0.1:3002, and tailscale serve puts it on the tailnet's port 80. Besides SSH, the VPS's only public ports are 80 and 443, which serve Uptime Kuma's badges and nothing else (see Uptime Kuma). Plain HTTP, because the System Activity panels load from Grafana at http://dashboard:3000 and an HTTPS page would block them; the tailnet encrypts the traffic anyway. Use the short name: for the full name dashboard.tail1e494e.ts.net, Chrome tries HTTPS first and warns or blocks, since the tailnet has HTTPS certificates off (single-label names are exempt).

tailscale serve cannot proxy to the sites' subnets itself (tailscaled's own connections don't use the subnet routes), so anything the browser needs from a site must be reachable from the browser directly. Grafana's panels don't need that: Grafana runs on the VPS and queries the sites from its container, which does use the routes.

The VPS joins the tailnet as a client named dashboard that accepts the sites' subnet routes, which is how its widgets reach 10.2.x.x and 10.3.x.x. Its Tailscale values are in site_ovh/infra_dashboard/tailscale.yml. The VPS is its own site, ovh, so it inherits nothing from the lab sites (in site_wil it would pick up wil-gateway's subnet-router settings).

docs.title: Container Configuration
docs.text:
• Memory: 512MB limit, 256MB reservation
  • Ports: 127.0.0.1:3002 only
  • Environment: receives API keys for service widgets (Sonarr, Radarr, Bazarr, Prowlarr, SABnzbd, Plex); compose.yaml is root-only (0600)

docs.title: Configuration Reference
docs.text: Parameter Type Description Default homepage_image string Docker image for Homepage ghcr.io/gethomepage/homepage:latest homepage_allowed_hosts string Comma-separated hostnames Homepage responds to dashboard.tail1e494e.ts.net,dashboard

docs.title: Dashboard Configuration
docs.text:
Homepage is configured via four YAML template files and a stylesheet:

File Purpose services.yaml.j2 Service cards: a small card per service for the Overview tab, and the full cards with widgets for the site tabs (Grafana graphs, media, apps, infrastructure, monitoring) bookmarks.yaml.j2 Empty: every link is a card on the Overview tab. The file stays, because Homepage writes its example bookmarks when it is missing settings.yaml.j2 Theme (light, gray), status dots, tabs (Overview, wil, ldn, ovh), group icons, layout (row style, column counts) widgets.yaml.j2 Global widgets (the VPS's resources, search bar, datetime) files/homepage/custom.css The look: the layout of a dashboard shared in Homepage's "Share your homepage" thread in the colours of samuel.computer (sky page, frosted-glass header, white cards, olive accents, Inter)

The dashboard has four tabs:

Tab Shows Overview Every service of all three sites as a small card (icon, link, status dot), in the groups Media, Apps, Infrastructure and Monitoring. Opens first wil wil in full: System Activity graphs, the media stack's cards with their widgets, apps, infrastructure, Prometheus and the node exporters ldn The same for ldn ovh The VPS's own services: Grafana, Uptime Kuma, Kanidm

services.yaml.j2 is plain Homepage YAML; edit it directly. These parts are less obvious:

  • Two cards per service: Homepage shows a group on one tab only, so each service is written twice: a small card (icon, href, siteMonitor) in an Overview group, and its full card (with description and widgets) in its site's group. Change a link or a status URL in both.
  • Links: a small card's href ends in / and its full card's doesn't. Quick launch (start typing on the page) lists both cards, and two entries with the same name and the same link make it show results that no longer match what was typed.
  • Group names are unique across the file, because Homepage finds a card by its group's name. That is why most groups on the site tabs carry their site: Infrastructure (wil), Apps (ldn), Services (ovh). A new group needs a matching entry in the layout of settings.yaml.j2, with the tab it belongs on; a group left out of layout shows on every tab.
  • Status dots: siteMonitor requests the URL from the VPS and counts any answer up to 403 as up. KOSync's small card has none: it answers 412 to a request without KOReader's Accept header, so only its full card checks it, with a customapi widget that sends the header.
  • Tile colours: a widget's highlight rules mark tiles good, warn or danger, and custom.css tints them lime, orange or pink (Homepage's own tints lose to the tile background). Used for Prometheus targets down, Uptime Kuma sites down, Tdarr errors, Prowlarr failed grabs and KOSync health.
  • System Activity shows the four panels of the System Activity Grafana dashboard on each site's tab, in iframes from http://dashboard:3000/d-solo/system-activity?var-ds=prometheus-<site>&panelId=1 to 4, in Grafana's light theme (theme=light). var-ds picks the site's Prometheus. Grafana allows anonymous viewing and embedding. The time range and refresh interval come from the dashboard JSON.
  • Node exporters follow Prometheus in each site's Monitoring group: a few VMs per site, listed by hand in services.yaml.j2. Prometheus itself scrapes every host of the site (prometheus_node_targets); a new VM gets a tile only when it is added to that list.
  • Five cards in a row (columns: 5: the Overview groups and the Monitoring groups) become four in a window 1024px to 1279px wide, where five are too narrow (custom.css). Narrower windows get Homepage's own two in a row, then one.
  • SABnzbd has two widgets: Homepage's sabnzbd widget (speed, queue) and a customapi widget that reads the download totals for today, this week, this month and all time from SABnzbd's server_stats API once a minute.

Sources: ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_ovh/infra_dashboard/vars.yml · ansible/playbooks/infrastructure/dashboard/templates/homepage/services.yaml.j2

docs.title: Uptime Kuma
docs.text: Uptime Kuma runs next to Homepage on the OVH VPS, in the same compose project (/opt/dashboard, state in /var/lib/dashboard/uptime-kuma), so its checks keep running when a site is down. It reaches the sites over the tailnet like Homepage's widgets, and the internet directly. The status badges in the repository's README come from it.

docs.title: Access
docs.text:
• Admin page: tailnet only, http://dashboard:3001. Uptime Kuma listens on 127.0.0.1:3001 and tailscale serve puts it on the tailnet's port 3001. The first visit asks for the admin account. UPTIME_KUMA_DB_TYPE=sqlite skips the database question that Uptime Kuma 2 asks first.
  • Badges: public, https://uptime.ext.5am.cloud/api/badge/.... Caddy (files/Caddyfile) passes /api/badge/* to Uptime Kuma and answers 404 for everything else, the login and status pages included. It gets its certificate from Let's Encrypt, so ports 80 and 443 are open on the VPS's public address (only there: tailscale serve holds port 80 on the tailnet address).
  • DNS: uptime.ext.5am.cloud is a DNS-only A record in Cloudflare pointing at 135.148.219.216, and wil's BIND serves the same address to the lab (site_wil/proxy/ext.5am.cloud.yml, applied by a wil networking deploy).

Monitors and status pages live in Uptime Kuma's database, not in Ansible: add them on the admin page.

docs.title: Badges
docs.text:
Uptime Kuma only draws a badge for a monitor that is on a published status page; any other monitor ID returns a grey N/A. Every monitor with a badge goes on the status page with the slug default, which Homepage's Uptime Kuma widget reads too. The page itself isn't reachable from the internet; publishing it only lets the badges show.

Badge URL Up / Down https://uptime.ext.5am.cloud/api/badge/<id>/status?label=<name> Uptime % https://uptime.ext.5am.cloud/api/badge/<id>/uptime/<duration>?label=<name> (24h, 7d, 30d; set label, the default one reads Uptime (30h) for 30d) Response time https://uptime.ext.5am.cloud/api/badge/<id>/ping/<duration> Certificate expiry https://uptime.ext.5am.cloud/api/badge/<id>/cert-exp

The monitor ID is the number at the end of its URL on the admin page (/dashboard/<id>). Badges are sent with Cache-Control: no-store, so GitHub's image proxy shows the current state (Uptime Kuma caches each badge for 5 minutes itself).

docs.text:

The badge proxy is Caddy built from networking/templates/Dockerfile.j2 (the sites' build, with the Cloudflare DNS plugin that Kanidm's auth.5am.cloud certificate needs), and its version is pinned there.

docs.text:
Node exporter targets come from the inventory: every host under [site_<env>] in ansible/inventory/hosts.ini is scraped on :9100 (the Packer template installs node-exporter on every clone). A host that is in the inventory but down shows as a target that is down.

docs.text:
1. Edit ansible/playbooks/infrastructure/dashboard/templates/homepage/services.yaml.j2

docs.text:
1. On http://dashboard:3001, add the monitor and put it on the default status page (Edit Status Page → add the monitor → Save)
  2. Note its ID from the address bar (/dashboard/<id>)

  3. Add the badge to README.md:

    ![wil](https://uptime.ext.5am.cloud/api/badge/<id>/status?label=wil)

No deploy needed: monitors live in Uptime Kuma's database.

docs.title: Networking
docs.text:
The networking stack provides DNS resolution, reverse proxying, dynamic DNS, and VPN connectivity across all environments. It deploys as a single Ansible playbook and is the first infrastructure service to run — all other services depend on it.

Deploy networking first

The networking playbook must run before any other service. DNS and reverse proxy availability are prerequisites for CA, NTP, monitoring, and all application deployments.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
graph TD
    subgraph External
        ExtClient[External Client]
        CloudflareDNS[Cloudflare DNS]
        DDNS[Cloudflare DDNS]
    end

    subgraph Internal
        UDM[UDM Pro Gateway]
        Client[Internal Client]
        BIND9[BIND9 DNS]
        Caddy[Caddy Reverse Proxy]
        Backend[Backend Service]
    end

    Client -->|1. DNS query| BIND9
    BIND9 -->|"2a. proxied: true"| Caddy
    BIND9 -->|"2b. proxied: false"| Backend
    Caddy -->|3. reverse proxy| Backend
    ExtClient -->|DNS query| CloudflareDNS
    CloudflareDNS -->|public IP| UDM
    UDM -->|"port forward\n80/443"| Caddy
    DDNS -->|updates public IP| CloudflareDNS

Internal clients query BIND9 for service hostnames. Proxied services resolve to the Caddy reverse proxy IP, which terminates TLS and forwards to backends. Non-proxied services resolve directly to the backend IP. External clients resolve via Cloudflare DNS and reach Caddy over the public IP — the UDM Pro port-forwards ports 80/443 to Caddy, and DDNS keeps the public IP current.

docs.text: Component Purpose Docs UniFi UDM Pro Gateway, VLANs, static routes, port forwarding Gateway BIND9 Internal authoritative DNS with split-horizon resolution DNS Services Caddy Reverse proxy with automatic wildcard TLS via Cloudflare Reverse Proxy oauth2-proxy Login check in front of proxied services; users sign in with Kanidm on the VPS Single Sign-On Tailscale Encrypted WireGuard VPN mesh between sites VPN Cloudflare DDNS Updates public DNS records with current public IP Below

docs.text:
graph LR
    subgraph WIL["WIL (10.2.x.x)"]
        WIL_DNS["BIND9\n10.2.20.53"]
        WIL_Caddy["Caddy\n10.2.20.53"]

    end

        LDN_DNS["BIND9\n10.3.20.53"]

    WIL_TS <-->|"Tailscale Tunnel\n100.64.0.0/10"| LDN_TS
    WIL_DNS -->|"zone transfer\n(AXFR)"| LDN_DNS
    LDN_DNS -->|"zone transfer\n(AXFR)"| WIL_DNS

Each environment runs a UDM Pro gateway with VLANs and a networking VM at .53 on VLAN 20. WIL is the primary DNS for 5 domains; LDN is primary for ldn.5am.cloud. Each site replicates the other's zones as secondary via AXFR. Tailscale subnet routers provide L3 connectivity between sites over the CGNAT range (100.64.0.0/10), with static routes on the UDM Pro directing cross-site traffic to the Tailscale VM.

Environment Network DNS Server Domains (primary) WIL 10.2.0.0/16 10.2.20.53 5am.video, 5am.cloud, wil.5am.cloud, ext.5am.cloud, sfc.al LDN 10.3.0.0/16 10.3.20.53 ldn.5am.cloud

Infrastructure VMs use consistent IP suffixes across environments:

Service Suffix WIL IP LDN IP Networking (DNS, Caddy, Tailscale) .53 10.2.20.53 10.3.20.53 Certificate Authority (Step-CA) .9 10.2.20.9 10.3.20.9 NTP Server (Chrony) .123 10.2.20.123 10.3.20.123 Monitoring (Prometheus) .30 10.2.20.30 10.3.20.30

docs.title: Service Definition System
docs.text:
A unified YAML service model drives both DNS records and Caddy reverse proxy configuration. Each service is defined once and consumed by both BIND9 zone templates and the Caddyfile template.

graph LR
    A["Per-domain YAML
(proxy/5am.video.yml, etc.)"] --> B["services aggregation
(all/vars.yml)"]
    R["App registry
(apps.yml proxy: blocks)"] --> B
    B --> C["domain.zone.j2
(DNS A records)"]
    B --> D["Caddyfile.j2
(reverse proxy)"]

Service definitions come from two sources, both in the site's folder. Apps in the site's registry (group_vars/site_<env>/apps.yml) declare a proxy: block, from which entries are generated automatically. Manual per-domain files in ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_<env>/proxy/ cover services outside the catalog (third-party devices, media stack, monitoring). services in group_vars/all/vars.yml aggregates the domain lists (injecting the domain field), appends the registry-generated entries, and keeps only the zones of the host's site.

See Reverse Proxy — Service Definition Reference for the full field specification.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
Deploy the full networking stack:

task ansible:deploy-networking ENV=wil

The playbook targets the infra_networking host group and runs five components in order:

  1. Tailscale — VPN mesh (via role)
  2. BIND9 — DNS server configuration and zone files
  3. Cloudflare DDNS — dynamic DNS updater container
  4. oauth2-proxy — login check (users sign in with Kanidm), then the sync of Kanidm's redirect URLs
  5. Caddy — reverse proxy with TLS

docs.title: Deployment Order
docs.text:
Networking deploys first in the infrastructure stack. The dependency chain:

Networking → Step-CA → NTP → Monitoring → Applications

docs.title: Cloudflare DDNS
docs.text: Cloudflare DDNS runs as a Docker container using the favonia/cloudflare-ddns image in host network mode. It detects the public IP and updates specified Cloudflare DNS records.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Edit ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_<env>/infra_networking/ddns.yml:

ddns_domains:
  - "plex.5am.video"
  - "convert.wil.5am.cloud"

docs.title: ddns_domains
docs.text:
FQDNs to keep updated with the current public IP.

Type: list[string]

ddns_domains:
  - "plex.5am.video"

The container runs with minimal privileges (all capabilities dropped, read-only filesystem, no new privileges) and uses the CF_API_TOKEN from SOPS-encrypted secrets for Cloudflare API access.

docs.title: DNS Services (BIND9)
docs.text: BIND9 provides internal authoritative DNS with split-horizon resolution across all environments. Internal clients resolve service hostnames to local IPs, while external clients resolve via Cloudflare to public IPs.

docs.title: File Locations
docs.text: File Purpose ansible/playbooks/infrastructure/networking/tasks/bind9.yml Installation and configuration task ansible/playbooks/infrastructure/networking/templates/named.conf.j2 Main BIND9 configuration ansible/playbooks/infrastructure/networking/templates/domain.zone.j2 Per-domain zone file template ansible/playbooks/infrastructure/networking/templates/reverse.zone.j2 Reverse DNS zone template ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_<env>/infra_networking/bind9.yml Per-environment DNS variables ansible/inventory/group_vars/all/sites.yml Each site's DNS server and zones (domains and the zone transfer variables are derived from it)

docs.title: Split-Horizon DNS
docs.text:
The DNS server returns different IPs based on where the query originates:

graph TD
    Client[Internal Client] -->|"dig plex.5am.video"| BIND9
    ExtClient[External Client] -->|"dig plex.5am.video"| Cloudflare

    BIND9 -->|"proxied: true"| ProxyIP["reverse_proxy_ip\n(10.2.20.53)"]
    BIND9 -->|"proxied: false"| BackendIP["backend_host\n(direct IP)"]
    Cloudflare -->|"A record"| PublicIP["Public IP\n(via DDNS)"]
  • Proxied services (proxied: true) resolve to reverse_proxy_ip — traffic goes through Caddy for TLS termination and routing
  • Non-proxied services (proxied: false) resolve directly to backend_host — clients connect to the backend IP without Caddy

This logic lives in the domain.zone.j2 template:

{{ service.name }} IN A {{ reverse_proxy_ip if service.proxied else service.backend_host }}

docs.title: Local-Only Zones
docs.text:
wil.5am.cloud and ldn.5am.cloud are local-only: they have no records in the public Cloudflare zone and only resolve through BIND9. Public DNS records are created exclusively for the hostnames listed in ddns_domains (group_vars/site_<env>/infra_networking/ddns.yml), e.g. plex.5am.video and kosync.5am.cloud. Everything else must reach the internal BIND servers (directly on the LAN, or via Tailscale split DNS when roaming); a query that leaks to a public resolver returns NXDOMAIN rather than a wrong answer.

This works from either site because each BIND server holds every zone — master for its own site's zones and slave (via zone transfer) for the other's — so both 10.2.20.53 and 10.3.20.53 answer all local names. For this to hold, client VLANs must hand out the BIND servers via DHCP (see Gateway — DHCP DNS); never point clients at a public resolver.

BIND9 generates zone files from two data sources:

  1. domains — derived from the site's zones in group_vars/all/sites.yml, defines which zones this server is authoritative for
  2. services — aggregated service list provides A records within each zone. It is built (in group_vars/all/vars.yml) from two sources in the site's folder: manual per-domain lists in group_vars/site_<env>/proxy/<domain>.yml (non-catalog services) plus registry-generated entries from proxy: blocks in group_vars/site_<env>/apps.yml (see Reverse Proxy — Registry-Generated Entries)

For each domain, the domain.zone.j2 template generates:

  • SOA and NS records with the DNS server as nameserver
  • A records for every enabled service matching that domain
  • Serial number from the current epoch (auto-increments on each deploy)
  • TTL of 300 seconds (5 minutes)

Because of the serial, the zone files change on every deploy; BIND reloads them (rndc reload) and is restarted only when named.conf itself changes. Each file is checked before it replaces the live one, named.conf with named-checkconf and a zone with named-checkzone: a file BIND would refuse fails the deploy at that task and DNS keeps running on the old one.

WILLDN 
# derived from sites.wil.zones (group_vars/all/sites.yml)
domains:
  - name: "5am.video"
  - name: "5am.cloud"
  - name: "wil.5am.cloud"
  - name: "ext.5am.cloud"
  - name: "sfc.al"

# derived from sites.ldn.zones (group_vars/all/sites.yml)
domains:
  - name: "ldn.5am.cloud"

docs.title: Cross-Site Zone Transfers
docs.text:
WIL and LDN replicate each other's zones as secondaries via AXFR. When a zone changes on the primary, it notifies the secondary, which pulls the updated zone.

graph LR
    WIL["WIL DNS (10.2.20.53)\nPrimary: 5am.video, 5am.cloud,\nwil.5am.cloud, ext.5am.cloud, sfc.al"]
    LDN["LDN DNS (10.3.20.53)\nPrimary: ldn.5am.cloud"]

    WIL -->|"AXFR + notify"| LDN
    LDN -->|"AXFR + notify"| WIL
Zone Primary Secondary 5am.video WIL (10.2.20.53) LDN (10.3.20.53) 5am.cloud WIL (10.2.20.53) LDN (10.3.20.53) wil.5am.cloud WIL (10.2.20.53) LDN (10.3.20.53) ext.5am.cloud WIL (10.2.20.53) LDN (10.3.20.53) sfc.al WIL (10.2.20.53) LDN (10.3.20.53) ldn.5am.cloud LDN (10.3.20.53) WIL (10.2.20.53)

Zone transfer configuration is derived from each site's row in group_vars/all/sites.yml: a site replicates every other site's zones, with that site's dns and ts_router_ips as masters (cross-site NOTIFYs arrive from the tailnet IP), and allows transfers from and sends notifies to the other sites' dns:

WILLDN 
# WIL replicates ldn.5am.cloud from LDN
dns_secondary_zones:
  - name: "ldn.5am.cloud"
    masters:
      - "10.3.20.53"
      - "100.73.47.81"

dns_transfer_clients:
  - "10.3.20.53"
  - "100.64.0.0/10"

dns_notify_targets:
  - "10.3.20.53"

# LDN replicates all WIL zones
dns_secondary_zones:
  - name: "5am.video"
    masters:
      - "10.2.20.53"
      - "100.103.137.102"
  - name: "5am.cloud"
    masters:
      - "10.2.20.53"
      - "100.103.137.102"
  - name: "wil.5am.cloud"
    masters:
      - "10.2.20.53"
      - "100.103.137.102"
  - name: "ext.5am.cloud"
    masters:
      - "10.2.20.53"
      - "100.103.137.102"
  - name: "sfc.al"
    masters:
      - "10.2.20.53"
      - "100.103.137.102"

dns_transfer_clients:
  - "10.2.20.53"
  - "100.64.0.0/10"

dns_notify_targets:
  - "10.2.20.53"

Note

Cross-site zone transfers work over Tailscale. The CGNAT range (100.64.0.0/10) is included in both dns_trusted_networks and dns_transfer_clients to allow queries and transfers through the VPN tunnel.

docs.title: Cross-Site Query Flow
docs.text:
When an LDN client accesses a WIL service (e.g., plex.5am.video), the query is resolved locally from the replicated secondary zone — no live forwarding to WIL is needed. The resulting IP routes through Tailscale to reach WIL's Caddy.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client as LDN Client<br/>10.3.0.50
    participant LDNS as LDN BIND9<br/>10.3.20.53
    participant TS as Tailscale VPN<br/>100.64.x.x
    participant Caddy as WIL Caddy<br/>10.2.20.53
    participant Plex as Plex Server<br/>10.2.0.5

    Client->>LDNS: Query: plex.5am.video
    note over LDNS: Secondary zone for 5am.video<br/>(replicated from WIL via AXFR)
    LDNS-->>Client: A: 10.2.20.53

    Client->>TS: Connect to 10.2.20.53:443
    note over TS: UDM Pro static route<br/>10.2.0.0/16 → Tailscale subnet router
    TS->>Caddy: Route via WireGuard tunnel
    note over Caddy: TLS termination<br/>Match @plex host matcher
    Caddy->>Plex: Reverse proxy to 10.2.0.5:32400
    Plex-->>Caddy: Response
    Caddy-->>TS: Encrypted response
    TS-->>Client: Response

Key points:

  • No live DNS forwarding — LDN BIND9 answers from its local secondary copy of the 5am.video zone, so the query resolves instantly without crossing the VPN
  • Zone data reflects WIL's reverse_proxy_ip — the replicated A record points to 10.2.20.53 (WIL Caddy), not 10.3.20.53 (LDN Caddy)
  • Traffic routing — the UDM Pro static route sends 10.2.0.0/16 traffic to the Tailscale subnet router, which tunnels it to WIL
  • Full TLS chain — Caddy terminates TLS on the WIL side using the wildcard certificate for *.5am.video

docs.title: Reverse DNS (PTR Records)
docs.text:
Reverse DNS maps IP addresses back to hostnames. Each environment defines a reverse zone for its services subnet and a list of PTR records.

dns_reverse_zone: "20.2.10.in-addr.arpa"

dns_ptr_records:
  - octet: "9"
    hostname: "ca.wil.5am.cloud."
  - octet: "53"
    hostname: "dns.wil.5am.cloud."
  - octet: "123"
    hostname: "time.wil.5am.cloud."

The octet is the last octet of the IP address. The hostname must end with a trailing dot (.).

docs.title: Configuration Reference
docs.text:
All variables are set in ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_<env>/infra_networking/bind9.yml, except the ones marked (derived), which come from ansible/inventory/group_vars/all/sites.yml.

Parameter Type Description Default dns_forwarders list[string] Upstream DNS servers for recursive queries ["1.1.1.1", "1.0.0.1"] dns_trusted_networks list[string] Networks allowed to query and use recursion (derived) dns_secondary_zones list[object] Zones to replicate from remote primaries via AXFR (derived) dns_transfer_clients list[string] IPs/CIDRs allowed to pull AXFR zone transfers (derived) dns_notify_targets list[string] IPs to notify on zone changes (must be IPs, not CIDRs) (derived) dns_forward_zones list[string\|object] Zones to forward to external resolvers [] reverse_proxy_ip string IP for DNS A records of proxied services (Caddy IP) (per-env) dns_reverse_zone string Reverse DNS zone name (in-addr.arpa format) (per-env) dns_ptr_records list[object] PTR records mapping last IP octet to FQDN (trailing dot required) []

docs.title: Add a PTR record
docs.text:
1. Edit ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_<env>/infra_networking/bind9.yml

  2. Add an entry to dns_ptr_records:

    dns_ptr_records:
  # ... existing entries
  - octet: "60"
    hostname: "work.wil.5am.cloud."

  3. Deploy:

    task ansible:deploy-networking ENV=wil

docs.title: Add a forward zone
docs.text:
1. Edit ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_<env>/infra_networking/bind9.yml

  2. Add an entry to dns_forward_zones:

    dns_forward_zones:
  - name: "corp.example.com"
    forwarders:
      - "192.168.1.1"

  3. Deploy:

    task ansible:deploy-networking ENV=wil

docs.title: Configure zone transfer to a new secondary
docs.text:
There is nothing to set in bind9.yml: every site's BIND9 is a secondary for the other sites' zones, derived from group_vars/all/sites.yml. To add a site, or change a site's dns, ts_router_ips or zones, edit its row there, then deploy networking at every site:

task ansible:deploy-networking ENV=wil
task ansible:deploy-networking ENV=ldn

Ensure network connectivity between servers (direct or via Tailscale).

docs.title: Verify DNS resolution
docs.text:
# Query a specific DNS server
dig plex.5am.video @10.2.20.53

# Check a PTR record
dig -x 10.2.20.53 @10.2.20.53

# Verify zone transfer
dig AXFR 5am.video @10.2.20.53

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Service not resolving — Check BIND9 is running: ssh <networking-ip> systemctl status named. Verify the service has an entry in the correct domain file under group_vars/site_<env>/proxy/ (or a proxy: block on the app's entry in group_vars/site_<env>/apps.yml) and redeploy: task ansible:deploy-networking ENV=wil.

Wrong IP returned — If a proxied service resolves to backend_host instead of reverse_proxy_ip, check that proxied: true is set. If a non-proxied service resolves to the Caddy IP, check that proxied: false is set.

Zone transfer not working — Verify Tailscale connectivity between sites. Check that dns_transfer_clients (derived from group_vars/all/sites.yml) includes the remote DNS server IP and the CGNAT range. Test with dig AXFR <zone> @<primary-dns>.

Serial number not incrementing — Zone serials use the current epoch. If BIND9 doesn't pick up changes, reload it: ssh <networking-ip> sudo rndc reload.

docs.title: Reverse Proxy (Caddy)
docs.text: Caddy serves as the reverse proxy for all web-facing services. It runs as a Docker container with a custom-built image that includes the Cloudflare DNS plugin for automatic wildcard TLS certificates.

docs.title: File Locations
docs.text: File Purpose ansible/playbooks/infrastructure/networking/tasks/caddy.yml Installation and configuration task ansible/playbooks/infrastructure/networking/templates/Caddyfile.j2 Reverse proxy configuration ansible/playbooks/infrastructure/networking/templates/compose.yaml.j2 Docker Compose service definition ansible/playbooks/infrastructure/networking/templates/Dockerfile.j2 Custom xcaddy build with Cloudflare plugin ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_<env>/proxy/*.yml Manual per-domain service definitions (non-catalog services) ansible/inventory/group_vars/all/vars.yml Registry entry generation and service aggregation ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_<env>/apps.yml App registry — proxy: blocks generate service entries

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The Caddyfile is generated from the unified services list. For each domain, a wildcard server block (*.domain.tld) is created with:

  1. TLS configuration — Cloudflare DNS-01 ACME challenge for wildcard certificates
  2. Per-service matchers — named host matchers (@servicename) route requests to the correct backend
  3. Reverse proxy directives — each service gets a handle block with optional headers, encoding, and transport configuration

Only services with proxied: true and enabled: true (default) generate Caddy entries.

*.5am.video {
    tls { dns cloudflare ... }

    @plex host plex.5am.video
    handle @plex {
        reverse_proxy 10.2.0.5:32400
    }

    @sonarr host sonarr.5am.video
    handle @sonarr {
        reverse_proxy 10.2.0.5:8989
    }
}

docs.title: Applying Changes
docs.text:
A networking deploy that changes the Caddyfile reloads Caddy, it does not restart it (handler Reload caddy: caddy reload inside the container, fed the new file):

  • No request is refused, and the ones in flight finish on the old config.
  • Open websockets (Kasm desktops, Proxmox consoles, live views) are closed and reconnect.
  • A Caddyfile that Caddy refuses fails the deploy at that handler, with Caddy's message naming the line. The old config keeps serving: fix the entry and deploy again.

The container itself restarts only when its image or compose.yaml changes (handler Rebuild caddy). The proxy is then away for a moment, or for up to 10 seconds if a long request (a stream, a download) is in flight: Caddy waits for it and Docker stops waiting after 10 seconds.

docs.title: TLS Certificate Management
docs.text:
Caddy obtains wildcard certificates for each domain using the Cloudflare DNS-01 ACME challenge. This means:

  • No ports need to be publicly open for certificate validation
  • One wildcard cert covers all subdomains per domain (e.g., *.5am.video)
  • Certificates auto-renew before expiry

External traffic reaches Caddy via port forwarding on the UDM Pro (ports 80 and 443).

The custom Docker image is built with xcaddy to include the caddy-dns/cloudflare plugin. Two environment variables authenticate with Cloudflare:

Variable Source Purpose CF_API_TOKEN SOPS-encrypted secrets Cloudflare API token with DNS edit permissions CF_EMAIL SOPS-encrypted secrets Cloudflare account email

The Caddy container exposes ports 80, 443, and 2019 (admin API), and mounts persistent volumes for certificate storage.

docs.title: Service Definition Reference
docs.text:
Service entries come from two sources:

  1. App registry — apps in the site's registry group_vars/site_<env>/apps.yml declare a proxy: block, and registry_services (in group_vars/all/vars.yml) generates their entries automatically. See Registry-Generated Entries.
  2. Manual per-domain files — YAML files under ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_<env>/proxy/ (the site that is primary for the domain) for services outside the app registry: third-party devices (Proxmox, NAS, KVM, Haivision), the media stack, monitoring, Frigate, and cloud gaming. Each file defines a list variable (e.g., wil_services, video_services) that is aggregated into services.

The fields below apply to entries from both sources.

docs.title: name
docs.text:
Subdomain name. Combined with the domain to form the FQDN (e.g., plex becomes plex.5am.video).

Type: string

name: plex

docs.title: backend_host
docs.text:
IP address of the backend service.

Type: string

backend_host: 10.2.0.5

docs.title: backend_port
docs.text:
Port number of the backend service.

Type: integer

backend_port: 32400

docs.title: proxied
docs.text:
Controls both DNS resolution and Caddy proxy behavior:

  • true — DNS resolves to reverse_proxy_ip, Caddy reverse proxies to the backend
  • false — DNS resolves directly to backend_host, no Caddy entry generated

Type: boolean

proxied: true

docs.title: enabled
docs.text:
Set to false to disable both the DNS record and Caddy entry for this service. Useful for temporarily taking a service offline without removing its definition.

Type: boolean

Default: true

enabled: false

docs.title: dns
docs.text:
Controls DNS A record generation. Set to "external" to skip internal A record creation — useful for services that only need Cloudflare DNS records.

Type: string

Default: "internal"

dns: external

docs.title: tls_skip_verify
docs.text:
Skip TLS certificate verification when proxying to the backend. Use when the backend serves HTTPS with a self-signed certificate (e.g., Proxmox, Kasm).

Type: boolean

Default: false

tls_skip_verify: true

docs.title: forward_headers
docs.text:
Add X-Real-IP, X-Forwarded-For, and X-Forwarded-Proto headers to proxied requests. Enable when the backend needs the client's real IP address.

Type: boolean

Default: false

forward_headers: true

docs.title: host_header
docs.text:
Set to "upstream" to override the Host header with the upstream host and port. Required by services that validate the Host header (e.g., Plex).

Type: string

Default: not set

host_header: upstream

docs.title: encode
docs.text:
Enable response encoding. Reduces bandwidth for content-heavy services.

Type: string

Default: not set

encode: gzip

docs.title: read_buffer
docs.text:
Transport read buffer size in bytes. Increase for services with large response headers or streaming payloads.

Type: integer

Default: not set

read_buffer: 8192

docs.title: no_service_worker
docs.text:
Caddy answers the backend's /serviceworker.js itself, with a worker that replaces the backend's and handles no requests. Set on Kasm: its service worker passes every page navigation through itself, downloads included, and Firefox stops a service worker after 30 s idle even mid-download, so any download from a Kasm session that takes longer than 30 s fails. The backend loses only what its worker did (Kasm: an offline page). Browsers pick up the new worker the next time they open a page of the site.

Type: boolean

Default: false

no_service_worker: true

docs.title: auth
docs.text:
Require a login before proxying. Caddy checks for a session first and sends the browser to the site's login page if there is none. Works for a service on any domain.

Type: boolean

Default: false

auth: true

docs.title: Minimal service
docs.text:
A basic proxied web application:

- name: tools
  backend_host: 10.2.20.60
  backend_port: 8070
  proxied: true

docs.title: Media service with headers and encoding
docs.text:
Plex requires header forwarding, host header override, gzip encoding, and an increased read buffer:

- name: plex
  backend_host: 10.2.0.5
  backend_port: 32400
  proxied: true
  encode: gzip
  forward_headers: true
  host_header: upstream
  read_buffer: 8192

docs.title: Self-signed backend
docs.text:
Proxmox serves HTTPS with a self-signed certificate:

- name: vm
  backend_host: 10.2.20.7
  backend_port: 8006
  proxied: true
  tls_skip_verify: true

docs.title: DNS-only (non-proxied) service
docs.text:
A service that gets a DNS record pointing directly to its IP, with no Caddy proxy:

- name: hmg
  backend_host: 10.2.20.186
  backend_port: 443
  proxied: false

docs.title: Registry-Generated Entries
docs.text:
Apps in a site's registry (group_vars/site_<env>/apps.yml) declare their DNS and proxy configuration inline via a proxy: block. A site's networking reads only its own registry, so the domain must be one of that site's zones:

kasm:
  host_group: app_kasm
  # renovate: datasource=docker
  image: "lscr.io/linuxserver/kasm:1.18.1"
  port: 4443
  proxy:
    name: kasm             # Subdomain → kasm.wil.5am.cloud
    domain: wil.5am.cloud
    proxied: true          # Required — no default in the zone template
    tls_skip_verify: true

registry_services (in group_vars/all/vars.yml) is built from every proxy: block in the site's registry — on a top-level app or a one-level-nested sub-service (e.g., apps.work.microbin.proxy). For each block:

  • backend_host is derived — the first inventory host of the app's host_group. If the group has no hosts in the inventory, the render fails loudly rather than silently dropping the entry.
  • backend_port defaults to the sibling port — set backend_port inside the proxy: block to override it.
  • name, domain, and proxied are required — proxied has no default in the zone template.
  • Optional fields pass through unchanged — tls_skip_verify, forward_headers, host_header, encode, read_buffer, no_service_worker, auth, dns, and enabled behave exactly as in manual entries.

Apps without a proxy: block get no DNS record and no Caddy entry.

docs.title: Service Aggregation
docs.text:
services in group_vars/all/vars.yml aggregates the site's manual per-domain service lists (injecting the domain field) and appends the registry-generated entries, which already carry their domain from the proxy: block. Manual lists come first to keep zone and Caddyfile ordering stable. The result is then cut down to the zones of the host's site (its zones in group_vars/all/sites.yml):

services: >-
  {{
    (
      (video_services | default([]) | map('combine', {'domain': '5am.video'}) | list) +
      (cloud_services | default([]) | map('combine', {'domain': '5am.cloud'}) | list) +
      (wil_services | default([]) | map('combine', {'domain': 'wil.5am.cloud'}) | list) +
      (ext_services | default([]) | map('combine', {'domain': 'ext.5am.cloud'}) | list) +
      (sfc_services | default([]) | map('combine', {'domain': 'sfc.al'}) | list) +
      (ldn_services | default([]) | map('combine', {'domain': 'ldn.5am.cloud'}) | list) +
      registry_services
    ) | selectattr('domain', 'in', sites[site].zones) | list
  }}

A list may aggregate even when no domain file defines it — the default([]) keeps unused lists (e.g., sfc_services in WIL, whose services all live in the registry) as extension points.

Both BIND9 zone templates and the Caddyfile template consume the resulting services list.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text: Scenario Configuration Modern web app with standard HTTP backend proxied: true (no optional fields needed) Backend with self-signed HTTPS (Proxmox, Kasm) Add tls_skip_verify: true Backend needs client IP (analytics, rate limiting) Add forward_headers: true Backend validates Host header (Plex) Add host_header: upstream Bandwidth-heavy streaming service Add encode: gzip Large response headers or websocket streams Add read_buffer: 8192 (or higher) Service only accessible externally via Cloudflare Add dns: external Web UI that should sit behind the single sign-on login Add auth: true Temporarily take a service offline Set enabled: false

docs.title: Add a new service to an existing domain
docs.text:
Registry apps — add a proxy: block to the app's entry in its site's registry, ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_<env>/apps.yml:

myapp:
  host_group: app_myapp
  # renovate: datasource=docker
  image: "myimage:latest"
  port: 8080
  proxy:
    name: myapp
    domain: wil.5am.cloud
    proxied: true

backend_host and backend_port are derived from the app's host_group and port — no manual entry is needed.

Non-catalog services (third-party devices, media stack, monitoring) — add an entry to the domain file, e.g., ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_wil/proxy/wil.5am.cloud.yml:

- name: myapp
  backend_host: 10.2.20.60
  backend_port: 8080
  proxied: true

Then, for either path:

  1. Deploy:

    task ansible:deploy-networking ENV=wil

  2. Verify:

    # Check DNS
dig myapp.wil.5am.cloud @10.2.20.53

# Check HTTPS
curl -I https://myapp.wil.5am.cloud

docs.title: Add a new domain
docs.text:
1. Add the domain to the site's zones in ansible/inventory/group_vars/all/sites.yml:

    sites:
  wil:
    # ...
    zones: [5am.video, 5am.cloud, wil.5am.cloud, ext.5am.cloud, sfc.al, new.5am.cloud]

  2. Create a service file in that site's folder, ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_wil/proxy/new.5am.cloud.yml:

    ---
new_services:
  - name: app
    backend_host: 10.2.20.60
    backend_port: 8080
    proxied: true

  3. Add the new list to services in ansible/inventory/group_vars/all/vars.yml:

    services: >-
  {{
    (
      ... +
      (new_services | default([]) | map('combine', {'domain': 'new.5am.cloud'}) | list) +
      registry_services
    ) | selectattr('domain', 'in', sites[site].zones) | list
  }}

  4. Ensure the domain is registered with Cloudflare (required for TLS certificates)

  5. Deploy networking at every site (the other sites become secondaries for the new zone):

    task ansible:deploy-networking ENV=wil
task ansible:deploy-networking ENV=ldn

docs.title: Disable a service temporarily
docs.text:
Set enabled: false on the service entry (for registry apps, inside the proxy: block in apps.yml). This removes both the DNS record and the Caddy proxy entry without deleting the configuration:

- name: myapp
  backend_host: 10.2.20.60
  backend_port: 8080
  proxied: true
  enabled: false

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
502 Bad Gateway — Caddy can reach the backend but it's not responding. Check the backend container is running: ssh <host> docker ps. Verify backend_port matches the container's exposed port. A service with auth: true also answers 502 while oauth2-proxy is down: check docker ps on the networking VM.

Certificate not issuing — Check Caddy logs: ssh <networking-ip> docker logs caddy. Common causes: Cloudflare API token expired, domain not on Cloudflare, or Let's Encrypt rate limit hit.

Service accessible via IP but not hostname — The DNS record is missing or pointing to the wrong IP. Check with dig <service>.<domain> @10.2.20.53 and verify the service entry in the domain file (or the app's proxy: block in apps.yml for registry apps).

Headers not forwarded — Ensure forward_headers: true is set on the service entry and redeploy networking.

Deploy fails at Reload caddy — Caddy refused the new Caddyfile and is still serving the old one. The error names the line of /opt/caddy/Caddyfile on the networking VM; fix the service entry it came from and redeploy networking.

docs.title: Single Sign-On (Kanidm)
docs.text: Kanidm on the OVH VPS is the one login for both sites, at https://auth.5am.cloud. It is reachable only over the tailnet. A proxied service opts in with auth: true in its service definition, on any domain. On each site's networking VM, oauth2-proxy runs next to Caddy as the login check.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Caddy asks oauth2-proxy before proxying a flagged service.
  2. No session for that domain: the browser is sent to Kanidm and comes back to the page it asked for.
  3. oauth2-proxy then sets a cookie for the service's domain, so the other flagged services on that domain open directly.
  4. The first visit to a flagged service on another domain passes through Kanidm without asking for the password again.

The login is a gate in front of a service, not a replacement for its own login: a service that has its own (the NAS, for example) still asks for it. Sonarr, Radarr, Prowlarr, SABnzbd and Pulsarr have theirs turned off. Proxmox, the backup server and Kasm log in to Kanidm themselves.

Piece Where Kanidm OVH VPS, in the dashboard compose project: config /opt/dashboard/kanidm/server.toml, state /var/lib/dashboard/kanidm auth.5am.cloud 100.116.40.99, the VPS's tailnet address. tailscale serve --tcp=443 passes it to the VPS's Caddy on 127.0.0.1:8443, which proxies to Kanidm oauth2-proxy Each networking VM, /opt/oauth2-proxy, client oauth2-proxy-<site> kanidm-mail-sender OVH VPS, next to Kanidm: sends its mail through Fastmail as noreply@5am.cloud (Password Reset by Email)

The name is in wil's BIND (zone 5am.cloud, copied to ldn) and in the tailnet's split DNS, never in Cloudflare. The VPS's public address closes any connection for it.

docs.title: File Locations
docs.text:
