docs.title: Admin Access
docs.text:
The admin account idm_admin has no stored password. Reset it when you need it (it prints a new one):

ssh -t ubuntu@dashboard sudo docker exec -it kanidm kanidmd recover-account idm_admin

Run the CLI from Kanidm's image, at the server's version (kanidm_image):

alias kanidm='docker run --rm -it -e KANIDM_URL=https://auth.5am.cloud -v kanidm-cli:/root/.cache kanidm/tools:1.12.0 kanidm'

kanidm login -D idm_admin

A session allows changes only for a while after login; kanidm reauth -D idm_admin renews it. Log out when done: kanidm logout -D idm_admin.

docs.title: Add a User
docs.text:
kanidm person create <user> "<Display Name>"

kanidm person update <user> --mail <address>

kanidm group add-members sso_users <user>

kanidm person credential create-reset-token <user> --ttl 86400

Send them the link or QR code. It lasts 24 hours and opens only from a site LAN or the tailnet. They set a password there, and a TOTP code or a passkey if they like. For a forgotten password they use Recover Account on the login page (Password Reset by Email), or you run the last command again.

A password alone is enough: idm_all_persons has credential-type-minimum set to any, where Kanidm's default asks for a second factor. To require one, set it back with kanidm group account-policy credential-type-minimum idm_all_persons mfa.

Every member of sso_users can open every flagged service; there are no per-user rules. Proxmox, PBS and Kasm keep their own permissions: create the Proxmox user and role on each host as in Proxmox and on WIL's backup server as in Proxmox Backup Server, and add the Kasm user to Administrators after their first login as in Kasm.

docs.title: Password Reset by Email
docs.text:
Recover Account on the login page asks for an email address. When it matches a person's address in Kanidm, Kanidm emails them a reset link from noreply@5am.cloud. The page answers the same either way, so it gives away no addresses. The link lasts an hour and, like the login, opens only from a site LAN or the tailnet. To email someone a link yourself (this one lasts 24 hours):

kanidm person credential send-reset-token <user> --ttl 86400

Kanidm only queues the mail. kanidm-mail-sender, next to Kanidm in the dashboard compose project, checks the queue every 5 seconds and sends through Fastmail (smtps://smtp.fastmail.com), logged in with an app password that has SMTP access only. 5am.cloud is a domain in that Fastmail account, with noreply@5am.cloud as an alias and Fastmail's SPF and DKIM records in Cloudflare.

These parts live in Kanidm's database:

  • each person's address: kanidm person update <user> --mail <address>
  • service account mail-sender, a member of idm_message_senders and nothing else, with a read-write API token (kanidm_mail_sender_token): kanidm service-account create mail-sender "Mail Sender" idm_admins, kanidm group add-members idm_message_senders mail-sender, kanidm service-account api-token generate mail-sender "mail sender" --readwrite
  • the Recover Account link: kanidm system domain set-allow-account-recovery true, as admin, because idm_admin can't change domain settings (admin has no stored password either: kanidmd recover-account admin, then kanidm login -D admin)

kanidm system message-queue list shows each message as queued, or with the time it went out. To test sending on its own, the mail sender can mail any address; it ends with Success! (kanidm system message-queue send-test-message is refused in 1.12.0, even for admin):

ssh ubuntu@dashboard sudo docker exec -e RUST_LOG=info kanidm-mail-sender /sbin/kanidm-mail-sender -c /etc/kanidm/config -m /etc/kanidm/mail-sender -t <address>

The sender logs only warnings and errors (RUST_LOG=warn), so its log stays empty while all is well.

docs.title: Protect a Service
docs.text:
Add auth: true to the service entry (for registry apps, inside the proxy: block), then deploy networking:

- name: prometheus
  backend_host: 10.2.20.30
  backend_port: 9090
  proxied: true
  auth: true

task ansible:deploy-networking ENV=wil

Kanidm has no wildcard redirect URLs, so the deploy registers the service's /oauth2/callback with the oauth2-proxy-<site> client before Caddy starts sending users to the login. It does that from the machine running the deploy, which must reach auth.5am.cloud (the tailnet or a site LAN). When a service loses auth: true, its callback stays in Kanidm until you remove it:

kanidm system oauth2 remove-redirect-url oauth2-proxy-wil https://<name>.<domain>/oauth2/callback

Only browsers can log in. Leave auth off services that apps, devices or scripts talk to through the hostname (Plex, KOSync and MicroBin, for example). Anything else can still use a protected service's IP and port directly.

docs.title: Proxmox
docs.text:
Each site's Proxmox logs in to Kanidm with realm sso (the default realm), as client proxmox-wil or proxmox-ldn. The realm's settings live in Proxmox. vm keeps auth: true, so the first visit passes the gate and then Proxmox's own sign-in, the second time without a password.

The host must resolve auth.5am.cloud, which neither host's resolver does, so both have this in /etc/hosts:

100.116.40.99 auth.5am.cloud

The realm was added with this command (WIL shown; for LDN use site_ldn, 10.3.20.10 and proxmox-ldn). The client key comes from the site's secrets and is never printed:

sops decrypt --extract '["kanidm_proxmox_client_secret"]' ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_wil/secrets.sops.yml | ssh root@10.2.20.7 'key=$(cat); pveum realm add sso --type openid --issuer-url https://auth.5am.cloud/oauth2/openid/proxmox-wil --client-id proxmox-wil --client-key "$key" --username-claim preferred_username --autocreate 0 --default 1'

The username claim cannot be changed later. Then create each user and make it an admin:

pveum user add <user>@sso

pveum acl modify / --users <user>@sso --roles Administrator

Keep root@pam. It is the way in through https://<host-ip>:8006 when Kanidm or Caddy is down, and a few settings stay root-only, such as raw args or PCI passthrough without a mapping. The realm only works on the vm name, because that is its only redirect URL.

docs.title: Proxmox Backup Server
docs.text:
WIL's backup server (10.2.10.99, a container on the NAS; https://pbs.wil.5am.cloud) logs in the same way: realm sso (the default realm), client pbs-wil, pbs keeps auth: true. Its resolver does not know auth.5am.cloud either, so it has the same /etc/hosts line as the Proxmox hosts. The client was created as idm_admin:

kanidm system oauth2 create pbs-wil "Proxmox Backup (wil)" https://pbs.wil.5am.cloud

kanidm system oauth2 add-redirect-url pbs-wil https://pbs.wil.5am.cloud

kanidm system oauth2 update-scope-map pbs-wil sso_users openid profile email

kanidm system oauth2 prefer-short-username pbs-wil

Its secret is kanidm_pbs_client_secret in WIL's secrets. The realm, with the key piped from there:

sops decrypt --extract '["kanidm_pbs_client_secret"]' ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_wil/secrets.sops.yml | ssh root@10.2.10.99 'key=$(cat); proxmox-backup-manager openid create sso --issuer-url https://auth.5am.cloud/oauth2/openid/pbs-wil --client-id pbs-wil --client-key "$key" --username-claim preferred_username --autocreate false --default true'

Then each user, made an admin:

ssh root@10.2.10.99 proxmox-backup-manager user create <user>@sso

ssh root@10.2.10.99 proxmox-backup-manager acl update / Admin --auth-id <user>@sso

Keep root@pam: it is the way in through https://10.2.10.99:8007 when Kanidm or Caddy is down. Proxmox VE and backup clients reach PBS by IP and fingerprint, not through the pbs name, so the gate does not affect them.

docs.title: Kasm
docs.text:
Kasm has no auth: true, so a desktop left open does not depend on a cookie that runs out. It logs in to Kanidm as client kasm, with PKCE off because Kasm cannot send it. The settings on Kasm's side live in Kasm's database, under Access Management > Authentication > OpenID:

Field Value Enabled On Display Name Kanidm Auto Login On Hostname kasm.ldn.5am.cloud Client ID kasm Client Secret kanidm_kasm_client_secret from LDN's secrets Authorization URL https://auth.5am.cloud/ui/oauth2 Token URL https://auth.5am.cloud/oauth2/token User Info URL https://auth.5am.cloud/oauth2/openid/kasm/userinfo Scope openid and profile, one per line Username Attribute preferred_username Groups Attribute Empty: the login fails if it is set Debug Off: it turns off TLS checks and writes tokens to the logs Redirect URL Kasm fills this in: https://kasm.ldn.5am.cloud/api/oidc_callback

To copy the secret without showing it:

sops decrypt --extract '["kanidm_kasm_client_secret"]' ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_ldn/secrets.sops.yml | pbcopy

The first login creates a Kasm user in the default group; add it to Administrators as admin@kasm.local. A Kasm user created through one OpenID config cannot log in through another (OIDC login rejected: different OIDC ID expected for user), and a local user of the same name is refused (Non OIDC user): delete the old user first.

Kasm's own login page is at https://kasm.ldn.5am.cloud/#/staticlogin. It is the way in for admin@kasm.local, also when Kanidm is down.

docs.title: Upgrades and Backups
docs.text:
• Renovate opens one pull request for kanidm/server and kanidm/tools (the mail sender) but never merges it. Upgrade one minor version at a time and never back: run ssh ubuntu@dashboard sudo docker exec kanidm kanidmd domain upgrade-check, deploy the dashboard with the new tag (task ansible:deploy-dashboard ENV=ovh), and move the CLI alias to the same tag.
  • Kanidm backs up its database every night at 22:00 UTC and keeps the last 7, in /var/lib/dashboard/kanidm/backups on the VPS. Nothing copies them elsewhere yet.
  • Kanidm's domain, auth.5am.cloud, is permanent: changing it breaks passkeys and every client's tokens.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
• Each domain's cookie lasts 12 hours. When it has ended, an open app does not renew it by itself: it shows errors or its own login box (Proxmox says "Login failed"). Reload the page.
  • To log out of a domain, open /oauth2/sign_out on any flagged name of that domain.
  • If oauth2-proxy is down, flagged services answer 502. If Kanidm is down, domains that already have a cookie keep working and new logins fail. Unflagged services are not affected.
  • A site's LAN reaches 100.116.40.99 through a static route on its UDM to the site's networking VM. A tailnet device away from home finds the name through the tailnet's split DNS route for auth.5am.cloud.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Kanidm says the redirect URL is not valid — the service's callback is not in the client's list yet. Run the networking deploy for that site.

Every flagged service answers 502 after a deploy — oauth2-proxy is not running: ssh <networking-ip> docker ps, then docker logs oauth2-proxy. It must reach auth.5am.cloud, which the container's extra_hosts pins to the VPS.

auth.5am.cloud does not resolve — on a LAN it comes from the site's BIND; away from home, from the tailnet's split DNS route. Hosts that use neither need a pin: the Proxmox hosts and the backup server have the /etc/hosts line, and oauth2-proxy's container has it in extra_hosts.

Kasm's login ends in Internal Error — Kasm's log has the reason: ssh 10.3.20.50 'docker exec kasm docker logs --since 10m kasm_api 2>&1' | grep -E 'Failed to find|\(invalid_'. Failed to find groups attribute means Groups Attribute is not empty. The authorization code has already been used means the error page was reloaded: start again from the login page.

No reset email arrives — kanidm system message-queue list shows whether Kanidm queued it. Nothing queued: the address typed is not the person's mail, or Recover Account is off. Still queued: the mail sender is down or Fastmail refused it: ssh ubuntu@dashboard sudo docker logs kanidm-mail-sender.

Check a client secret without a login — send Kanidm's token endpoint a fake code with the client's ID and secret. 401 means the secret is wrong; 400 with invalid_request means the secret is right and only the code was rejected.

Kanidm's own log — ssh ubuntu@dashboard sudo docker logs kanidm.

docs.title: VPN (Tailscale)
docs.text: Tailscale creates an encrypted WireGuard mesh network between geographically distributed environments. Subnet routers on each site's networking VM advertise local subnets, enabling cross-site communication over the CGNAT range (100.64.0.0/10).

docs.title: File Locations
docs.text: File Purpose ansible/roles/tailscale/tasks/main.yml Installation, configuration, and authentication ansible/roles/tailscale/defaults/main.yml Default variable values ansible/roles/tailscale/handlers/main.yml Service restart handler

docs.title: Deployment Modes
docs.text: Tailscale supports two modes, controlled by tailscale_mode:

docs.title: Client
docs.text: Default mode. Joins the Tailscale mesh as a regular node. Accepts routes from subnet routers to reach other sites. Used by the dashboard VPS (dashboard, see Homepage).

docs.title: Subnet Router
docs.text:
Advertises local network routes to the mesh. Used on networking VMs to make an entire site reachable from other sites. Enables:

  • IP forwarding — net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 and net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1 via sysctl
  • NAT masquerade — iptables rule for 100.64.0.0/10 traffic so Tailscale clients can reach non-Tailscale hosts on the local network
  • Systemd override — ensures tailscaled starts after the network is online
graph LR
    subgraph WIL["WIL (10.2.0.0/16)"]
        WIL_SR["Subnet Router\n10.2.20.53"]
        WIL_VM["Local VMs"]
    end

    subgraph LDN["LDN (10.3.0.0/16)"]
        LDN_SR["Subnet Router\n10.3.20.53"]
        LDN_VM["Local VMs"]
    end

    WIL_SR <-->|"WireGuard Tunnel\n100.64.0.0/10"| LDN_SR
    WIL_SR --- WIL_VM
    LDN_SR --- LDN_VM
    WIL_VM -.->|"via subnet router"| LDN_VM

docs.title: Configuration Reference
docs.text:
All variables are set in the host or group vars for machines running Tailscale. Defaults are defined in ansible/roles/tailscale/defaults/main.yml.

The role joins a node with tailscale up once. On every later deploy it reads the node's settings (tailscale debug prefs) and, when the routes, tailscale_accept_routes, tailscale_accept_dns or tailscale_hostname differ from the vars, applies them with tailscale set. A settings change needs no re-authentication.

Parameter Type Description Default tailscale_mode string "client" or "subnet_router" (advertises routes, enables IP forwarding) "client" tailscale_auth_key string Auth key from Tailscale admin console (SOPS-encrypted) "" tailscale_advertise_routes list[string] CIDRs to advertise (subnet_router only, requires admin approval) [] tailscale_accept_dns boolean Accept DNS from Tailscale (disable on BIND9 hosts) true tailscale_accept_routes boolean Accept routes from other Tailscale nodes false tailscale_hostname string Hostname in the Tailscale admin console "{{ inventory_hostname }}" tailscale_force_reauth boolean Force re-authentication on next run false

docs.title: Cross-Site Connectivity
docs.text: Tailscale subnet routers enable three critical cross-site functions. For non-Tailscale devices on the local network to use these routes, the UDM Pro must have static routes pointing remote subnets at the Tailscale subnet router VM.

docs.title: DNS Zone Transfers
docs.text: WIL and LDN DNS servers replicate zones via AXFR. The BIND9 servers reach each other through Tailscale using their local IPs (e.g., WIL queries LDN at 10.3.20.53), which the subnet routers make routable. See DNS — Cross-Site Zone Transfers.

docs.title: Service Access
docs.text:
Services on one site can be accessed from the other. For example, a client in LDN can reach plex.5am.video because:

  1. LDN BIND9 has 5am.video as a secondary zone (replicated from WIL)
  2. The A record resolves to WIL's reverse_proxy_ip (10.2.20.53)
  3. Tailscale routes traffic to 10.2.20.53 through the WireGuard tunnel

docs.title: Trusted Network Configuration
docs.text:
Both sites include the Tailscale CGNAT range in their BIND9 trusted networks, which are derived in group_vars/all/sites.yml:

dns_trusted_networks:
  - 100.64.0.0/10  # Tailscale CGNAT

This allows DNS queries and zone transfers originating from Tailscale IPs.

docs.title: DNS Integration
docs.text:
Networking VMs run both BIND9 and Tailscale. To prevent Tailscale from overriding the local DNS configuration:

tailscale_accept_dns: false

Without this, Tailscale would push its own DNS servers (MagicDNS), which would conflict with the locally running BIND9 instance.

Split DNS entries in the Tailscale admin console route domain queries to the correct BIND9 server per site:

docs.title: Security
docs.text: Aspect Implementation Encryption All traffic uses WireGuard encryption (always on) Authentication Auth keys stored as SOPS-encrypted secrets NAT traversal Coordinated by Tailscale control plane; no public ports needed IP forwarding Enabled only on subnet routers, not clients DNS isolation Subnet routers disable Tailscale DNS to avoid BIND9 conflicts Access control Tailscale ACLs control which nodes can communicate

docs.title: Set up a new subnet router
docs.text:
1. Set the Tailscale variables in the host's group vars:

    tailscale_mode: "subnet_router"
tailscale_auth_key: "{{ tailscale_auth_key_secret }}"
# The site's LAN from sites.yml, plus the subnets of VPN clients enabled on this VM
tailscale_advertise_routes: >-
  {{ [sites[site].cidr]
     + (vpn_clients | default([]) | selectattr('enabled') | map(attribute='routed_subnets') | flatten) }}
tailscale_accept_dns: false
tailscale_accept_routes: true

  2. Deploy:

    task ansible:deploy-networking ENV=wil

  3. Approve the advertised routes in the Tailscale admin console

docs.title: Change the advertised routes
docs.text:
tailscale_advertise_routes is derived: the site's cidr in group_vars/all/sites.yml, plus the routed_subnets of every VPN client enabled on the VM (vpn_clients.yml). Change the source, then:

  1. Deploy networking at that site: task ansible:deploy-networking ENV=<env>. The task "Apply changed Tailscale settings" reports changed when the node's routes differed.
  2. Approve any new route in the Tailscale admin console. A removed route needs no approval.

docs.title: Add a new site
docs.text:
1. Set up Tailscale on the new site's networking VM as a subnet router (see above)
  2. On existing sites, ensure tailscale_accept_routes: true so they accept the new site's routes
  3. Add static routes on each site's UDM Pro pointing the new subnet at the local Tailscale VM
  4. Add the new site's row to group_vars/all/sites.yml; every DNS server then trusts its subnet and exchanges zones with it (see DNS — Configure zone transfer to a new secondary)
  5. Deploy networking at every site

docs.title: Force re-authentication
docs.text:
If a node's auth key expires or the node needs to rejoin:

  1. Set tailscale_force_reauth: true in the host's vars

  2. Deploy:

    task ansible:deploy-networking ENV=wil

  3. Reset tailscale_force_reauth: false after successful authentication to avoid re-authing on every future run

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Cross-site traffic not routing — Verify the subnet router is advertising routes: ssh <networking-ip> tailscale status. Check that routes are approved in the Tailscale admin console. Verify UDM Pro static routes point to the correct next hop.

"login required" on deploy — The auth key has expired. Generate a new one from the Tailscale admin console, update the SOPS-encrypted secret, and redeploy with tailscale_force_reauth: true.

DNS queries failing over Tailscale — Ensure 100.64.0.0/10 is in dns_trusted_networks on the target DNS server. Check that tailscale_accept_dns: false is set on networking VMs to prevent MagicDNS from overriding BIND9.

docs.title: Gateway (UniFi)
docs.text: Each site runs a UniFi Dream Machine Pro (UDM Pro) as the network gateway. The UDM Pro handles VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, static routes for Tailscale, and port forwarding for the reverse proxy. Gateway configuration is managed manually through the UniFi controller UI — it is not automated via Ansible.

docs.title: VLANs
docs.text:
Each environment uses the same VLAN layout with environment-specific IP ranges.

WILLDN VLAN Name Subnet Purpose 1 Infrastructure 10.2.0.0/24 Proxmox hosts, NAS, physical infrastructure 10 Storage 10.2.10.0/24 Dedicated storage traffic 20 Virtual Machines 10.2.20.0/24 All Ansible-managed VMs 30 Servers Misc 10.2.30.0/24 Miscellaneous server devices 200 Wired Devices 10.2.200.0/24 Wired client devices 230 Wireless Devices 10.2.230.0/24 Wi-Fi client devices 245 IoT Devices 10.2.245.0/24 IoT and smart home devices VLAN Name Subnet Purpose 1 Infrastructure 10.3.0.0/24 Proxmox hosts, NAS, physical infrastructure 20 Virtual Machines 10.3.20.0/24 All Ansible-managed VMs 30 Servers Misc 10.3.30.0/24 Bare-metal lab devices (PTP time server and clients)

All Ansible-managed infrastructure and application VMs live on VLAN 20 (Virtual Machines). The networking VM at .53, CA at .9, NTP at .123, and monitoring at .30 are all on this VLAN. In LDN, the PTP time server (LattePanda MU) is a physical host on VLAN 30 at 10.3.30.123, managed by the separate ptp-experiments repo.

docs.title: DHCP DNS
docs.text:
Every client VLAN's DHCP must hand out the local BIND9 server as DNS — never Auto (which forwards to the WAN resolver) or a public resolver. wil.5am.cloud and ldn.5am.cloud are local-only zones with no public records, so a client pointed at Cloudflare gets NXDOMAIN for them.

In the UniFi controller: Settings → Networks → (network) → DHCP Service Management → DNS Server → Manual

WILLDN Field Value DNS Server 1 10.2.20.53 (local BIND) DNS Server 2 10.3.20.53 (LDN BIND, cross-site fallback) Field Value DNS Server 1 10.3.20.53 (local BIND) DNS Server 2 10.2.20.53 (WIL BIND, cross-site fallback)

The cross-site secondary is a valid fallback because each BIND server slaves the other site's zones (so it answers all local names) and the static routes make it reachable through the Tailscale tunnel. Clients pick up the new servers on lease renewal or reconnect.

Note

Devices with hardcoded DNS or browser DNS-over-HTTPS bypass DHCP entirely — those resolve local-only zones as NXDOMAIN regardless of this setting.

docs.title: mDNS
docs.text:
Ubuntu VMs cloned from the Packer template run avahi-daemon, so each one answers to <hostname>.local (the Terraform name, e.g. gaming.local) with no DNS record and no per-VM configuration. mDNS is link-local multicast: it only reaches the VM's own VLAN unless the gateway reflects it, and it never crosses Tailscale.

In the UniFi controller: Settings → Networks → (network) → Advanced → Multicast DNS — enable it on VLAN 20 and on every client VLAN that should resolve .local names. Older controllers have a single global toggle under Settings → Services → mDNS instead.

With that on, ssh gaming.local works from a client VLAN as soon as a new clone has booted. To drop the suffix and type ssh gaming, let ssh try .local for bare names in ~/.ssh/config:

Host *
    CanonicalizeHostname yes
    CanonicalDomains local

Note

Names are per site because each gateway reflects only its own VLANs: networking.local is the LDN VM when you are in LDN and the WIL VM when you are in WIL. Over Tailscale, mDNS does not work at all — reach VMs by IP through the subnet router instead.

docs.title: Static Routes
docs.text: Static routes on the UDM Pro direct traffic for remote site subnets through the local Tailscale subnet router. Without these routes, traffic destined for other sites would be sent to the default gateway (the ISP) instead of through the Tailscale tunnel.

docs.title: Why Static Routes Are Needed
docs.text:
The Tailscale subnet router VM advertises remote subnets to the Tailscale mesh, but the UDM Pro doesn't participate in Tailscale. Other VMs and physical devices on the network need a route to reach the remote subnets, so the UDM Pro must be told to forward that traffic to the Tailscale subnet router.

graph LR
    Client["Local Client\n(any VLAN)"] -->|"10.3.x.x"| UDM["UDM Pro"]
    UDM -->|"static route"| TSRouter["Tailscale Subnet Router\n10.2.20.53"]
    TSRouter -->|"WireGuard tunnel"| Remote["Remote Site\n10.3.x.x"]

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
In the UniFi controller: Settings → Routing → Static Routes

WILLDN Name Destination Next Hop Purpose LDN Network 10.3.0.0/16 10.2.20.53 Route to LDN via Tailscale Tailscale CGNAT 100.64.0.0/10 10.2.20.53 Route to Tailscale mesh IPs Name Destination Next Hop Purpose WIL Network 10.2.0.0/16 10.3.20.53 Route to WIL via Tailscale Tailscale CGNAT 100.64.0.0/10 10.3.20.53 Route to Tailscale mesh IPs

Note

The next hop is always the Tailscale subnet router VM (.53 on VLAN 20). This VM runs Tailscale in subnet_router mode with IP forwarding and NAT masquerade enabled. See VPN (Tailscale) — Deployment Modes.

docs.title: Adding a New Site Route
docs.text:
When adding a new site to the homelab:

  1. Deploy Tailscale on the new site's networking VM as a subnet router (see Tailscale — Set up a new subnet router)
  2. On each existing site's UDM Pro, add a static route:
    • Destination: the new site's subnet (e.g., 10.4.0.0/16)
    • Next Hop: the local Tailscale subnet router (e.g., 10.2.20.53)
  3. On the new site's UDM Pro, add static routes for each existing site

docs.title: Port Forwarding
docs.text: Port forwarding rules on the UDM Pro direct inbound internet traffic to the Caddy reverse proxy. This is required for external access to services like Plex and for Caddy to serve HTTPS on the public IP.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
In the UniFi controller: Settings → Firewall & Security → Port Forwarding

Name External Port Internal IP Internal Port Protocol Purpose HTTP 80 10.2.20.53 80 TCP HTTP → Caddy (redirects to HTTPS) HTTPS 443 10.2.20.53 443 TCP HTTPS → Caddy (reverse proxy)

Both rules forward to the networking VM (.53) where Caddy listens. Caddy handles TLS termination using wildcard certificates obtained via the Cloudflare DNS-01 challenge and routes requests to the appropriate backend service.

Warning

Only ports 80 and 443 should be forwarded. Individual services should never be directly exposed — all external traffic routes through Caddy. Services that need external access are configured with Cloudflare DDNS records pointing to the public IP.

docs.title: Traffic Flow
docs.text:
graph LR
    Internet[Internet Client] -->|"plex.5am.video:443"| UDM["UDM Pro\n(port forward)"]
    UDM -->|443| Caddy["Caddy\n10.2.20.53"]
    Caddy -->|"reverse proxy"| Plex["Plex\n10.2.0.5:32400"]
  1. External client resolves plex.5am.video via Cloudflare DNS → public IP
  2. UDM Pro receives traffic on port 443, forwards to 10.2.20.53:443
  3. Caddy terminates TLS, matches the hostname, and proxies to the backend

docs.title: Network Boot (PXE)
docs.text:
The LDN netboot VM (10.3.20.60) runs netboot.xyz for PXE re-imaging of bare-metal devices — currently the PTP time server on VLAN 30. See the Re-image the Time Server runbook.

In the UniFi controller: Settings → Networks → (VLAN 30 network) → DHCP Service Management → Show Options → Network Boot

Network Server Filename Purpose LDN VLAN 30 10.3.20.60 netboot.xyz.efi UEFI x86_64 PXE boot → netboot.xyz menu

Scoping the option to VLAN 30 keeps PXE away from every other network. If the controller version lacks a Network Boot toggle, set custom DHCP options 66 (TFTP server) and 67 (boot filename) instead.

docs.title: DHCP Reservation
docs.text:
The installed OS pins the time server's address statically by its PXE NIC's MAC (see the timeserver_hosts entry in the netboot vars); the installer itself uses DHCP only transiently to fetch the ISO. A fixed-IP reservation is kept purely as a backstop:

Device Fixed IP Notes LattePanda MU (PTP grandmaster) 10.3.30.123 Reserve against the PXE NIC MAC (40:a6:b7:81:7c:51), the same key as its timeserver_hosts entry

docs.title: Firewall Requirements
docs.text:
PXE clients on VLAN 30 must reach the netboot VM on VLAN 20: UDP 69 (TFTP) and TCP 8080 (HTTP boot assets). Inter-VLAN routing is allowed by default; only restrictive custom LAN-to-LAN rules would break this (symptom: iPXE times out fetching the boot file).

Raspberry Pi CM5 clients on the same VLAN ignore the boot filename option (netboot.xyz.efi is x86-only and harmless to them) and pin the TFTP server via TFTP_IP in their EEPROM instead of relying on this DHCP option — no UniFi changes are needed for them. See Provision a CM5.

docs.title: Inter-VLAN Routing
docs.text:
The UDM Pro routes traffic between VLANs by default. Key inter-VLAN traffic patterns:

Source Destination Purpose VLAN 200/230 (clients) VLAN 20 (VMs) Access services via Caddy VLAN 1 (infrastructure) VLAN 20 (VMs) Proxmox managing VMs VLAN 20 (VMs) VLAN 1 (infrastructure) VMs accessing NAS storage VLAN 20 (VMs) VLAN 10 (storage) Dedicated storage traffic (NFS/iSCSI) VLAN 245 (IoT) VLAN 20 (VMs) IoT devices reaching Home Assistant

Tip

Firewall rules on the UDM Pro can restrict inter-VLAN traffic. For example, IoT devices on VLAN 245 might only be allowed to reach specific IPs on VLAN 20 (like Home Assistant) and nothing else.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Cross-site traffic not reaching destination — Verify the static route exists in the UniFi controller (Settings → Routing → Static Routes). The next hop must be the Tailscale subnet router VM (.53). Check that the subnet router VM is running and Tailscale is connected.

Port forwarding not working — Verify the rules in Settings → Firewall & Security → Port Forwarding. Ensure ports 80 and 443 forward to the networking VM IP. Check that no firewall rules are blocking inbound traffic.

Inter-VLAN access denied — Check UniFi firewall rules. By default, inter-VLAN routing is allowed, but custom rules may restrict it. Verify the source and destination VLANs in the firewall policy.

docs.title: Time Server (Chrony)
docs.text:
Chrony provides NTP time synchronization for all infrastructure nodes. It runs as a native systemd service on a dedicated VM in each environment, synchronizing from upstream NTP servers and serving time to the local network.

Deployment order

NTP deploys after Networking and Step-CA, and before monitoring and applications.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
graph TD
    Upstream["Upstream NTP Servers\n(NIST, Cloudflare, etc.)"]
    Chrony["Chrony Server\n(.123)"]
    VM1[Infrastructure VMs]
    VM2[Application VMs]

    Upstream -->|sync| Chrony
    Chrony -->|serve time| VM1
    Chrony -->|serve time| VM2

The Chrony server synchronizes with multiple upstream NTP sources and acts as a stratum 10 local clock for the network. All VMs in the environment point to the local Chrony server instead of querying public NTP servers directly.

docs.title: File Locations
docs.text: File Purpose playbooks/infrastructure/ntp/deploy.yml Main playbook playbooks/infrastructure/ntp/tasks/chrony.yml Installation and configuration task playbooks/infrastructure/ntp/templates/servers.conf.j2 Upstream NTP server list playbooks/infrastructure/ntp/templates/allow.conf.j2 Client access allow list playbooks/infrastructure/ntp/templates/server.conf.j2 Server mode settings playbooks/infrastructure/ntp/handlers/main.yml Service restart handler inventory/group_vars/site_wil/infra_ntp/chrony.yml NTP variables

docs.title: Hosts
docs.text:
Environment IP FQDN WIL 10.2.20.123 time.wil.5am.cloud LDN 10.3.20.123 time.ldn.5am.cloud

These are the addresses set aside for a time server. Neither is in the inventory at the moment (wil's VM is gone), so [infra_ntp] is empty and deploy-ntp matches no host. To bring one back, add its address under [infra_ntp] and its [site_<env>] group in ansible/inventory/hosts.ini.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
task ansible:deploy-ntp ENV=wil

The task file:

  1. Installs chrony via apt
  2. Deploys upstream server configuration to /etc/chrony/conf.d/servers.conf
  3. Deploys client allow list to /etc/chrony/conf.d/allow.conf
  4. Deploys server mode config to /etc/chrony/conf.d/server.conf
  5. Enables and starts the chrony service
  6. Verifies synchronization with chronyc tracking
  7. Displays status output

docs.title: Server Mode Configuration
docs.text:
The server.conf.j2 template configures Chrony to operate as a local time source:

local stratum 10
rtcsync
hwtimestamp *
  • local stratum 10 — acts as a time source even if upstream servers are unreachable
  • rtcsync — synchronizes the system clock with the hardware clock
  • hwtimestamp * — enables hardware timestamping on all interfaces for precision

Sources: ansible/playbooks/infrastructure/ntp/tasks/chrony.yml · ansible/playbooks/infrastructure/ntp/templates/server.conf.j2

docs.title: Configuration Reference
docs.text:
All variables are set in ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_wil/infra_ntp/chrony.yml, which holds wil's values (NTP runs only at wil). An NTP host at another site needs its own copy in ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_<env>/infra_ntp/.

Parameter Type Description Default chrony_ntp_servers list[string] Upstream NTP servers (uses geographically local servers per-env) (per-env) chrony_allow list[string] Networks allowed to query this NTP server (per-env)

Sources: ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_wil/infra_ntp/chrony.yml · ansible/playbooks/infrastructure/ntp/templates/servers.conf.j2 · ansible/playbooks/infrastructure/ntp/templates/allow.conf.j2

docs.title: Verify time synchronization
docs.text:
SSH to the NTP server and check the tracking status:

chronyc tracking

Key fields to check:

  • Reference ID — upstream server currently in use
  • Stratum — should be 2-3 (one hop from the upstream stratum 1 server)
  • System time — offset from NTP time (should be sub-millisecond)

docs.title: Check connected clients
docs.text: chronyc clients

docs.title: Add a new upstream NTP server
docs.text:
1. Edit ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_wil/infra_ntp/chrony.yml:

    chrony_ntp_servers:
  # ... existing servers
  - time.google.com

  2. Deploy:

    task ansible:deploy-ntp ENV=wil

docs.title: Allow a new network
docs.text:
1. Add the network CIDR to chrony_allow:

    chrony_allow:
  - 10.2.0.0/16
  - 10.4.0.0/16    # new network

  2. Deploy:

    task ansible:deploy-ntp ENV=wil

docs.title: Ansible
docs.text: Ansible configures VMs and deploys services via Docker Compose.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
# Deploy everything
task ansible:deploy-all ENV=wil

# Deploy a specific service
task ansible:deploy-networking ENV=wil

# Deploy a data-driven app
task ansible:deploy-app ENV=ldn APP=kosync

# Test connectivity
task ansible:ping ENV=wil

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command Description deploy-all Full infrastructure deployment (runs site.yml; on ldn the final Proxmox play needs root SSH to the PVE host) deploy-networking BIND9, Caddy, oauth2-proxy, DDNS, Tailscale deploy-ca Step-CA certificate authority deploy-ntp Chrony NTP server deploy-monitoring Prometheus deploy-dashboard Grafana, Homepage, Uptime Kuma and Kanidm on the OVH VPS deploy-netboot netboot.xyz PXE re-imaging deploy-proxmox Proxmox hosts: SR-IOV GPU VFs, PCI resource mappings deploy-media Plex and *arr stack deploy-frigate Frigate NVR deploy-gaming Gaming stacks: Wolf and RomM (ldn) deploy-hermes Hermes Agent, Claude Code and the Claude subscription plugin deploy-app APP=<name> Single data-driven app ping Test connectivity to all hosts of the site

All commands require ENV=<env> and are prefixed with task ansible:.

docs.title: Playbook Pattern
docs.text:
Every playbook follows the same structure:

---
- name: Deploy <Service>
  hosts: <host_group>
  become: true

  handlers:
    - name: Include handlers
      ansible.builtin.import_tasks: handlers/main.yml

  pre_tasks:
    - name: Include common prerequisites
      ansible.builtin.include_role:
        name: common

  tasks:
    - name: Deploy service
      ansible.builtin.include_tasks: tasks/<taskname>.yml

The common role runs on every host first — it updates the apt cache and sets the timezone.

docs.title: Infrastructure Playbooks
docs.text:
Infrastructure services have dedicated playbooks in ansible/playbooks/infrastructure/:

Playbook Hosts Services networking/deploy.yml infra_networking BIND9, Caddy, oauth2-proxy, DDNS, Tailscale ca/deploy.yml infra_ca Step-CA ntp/deploy.yml infra_ntp Chrony monitoring/deploy.yml infra_monitoring Prometheus dashboard/deploy.yml infra_dashboard Tailscale, Grafana, Homepage, Uptime Kuma (OVH VPS) apps/kasm/deploy.yml app_kasm Kasm on the work VM (ldn), workspace images from files/ apps/kasm-agent/deploy.yml app_kasm_agent Second Kasm agent for Deluge (OVH VPS) netboot/deploy.yml infra_netboot netboot.xyz proxmox/deploy.yml infra_proxmox SR-IOV GPU VFs and PCI mappings on the hypervisor (no common role: it is not an Ubuntu VM)

docs.title: Data-Driven Apps
docs.text:
Most applications use the shared deploy-app.yml playbook. Apps are defined in the registry of the site that hosts them, ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_<env>/apps.yml:

kosync:
  host_group: app_kosync
  # renovate: datasource=docker
  image: "koreader/kosync:v2.1.1"
  port: 17200
  proxy:
    name: kosync
    domain: ldn.5am.cloud
    proxied: true

The deploy-app.yml playbook reads the app config, includes the docker_service role, and deploys the Docker Compose template from ansible/playbooks/apps/<name>/templates/compose.yaml.j2. The image pre-pull list is derived from every registry key ending in image (top level and one nesting level down) — there is no manual images: list. See Config Reference — App Registry for the full schema.

docs.title: Custom App Playbooks
docs.text:
Apps that need more than Docker Compose (e.g., media stack with NFS mounts) have custom playbooks at ansible/playbooks/apps/<name>/deploy.yml.

App Reason for Custom Playbook Media stack NFS mount, complex multi-container setup Frigate NFS mount, dedicated compose/config tasks Gaming Stacks selected per environment (Wolf and RomM), kernel modules and udev rules, GPU render-node check, Wolf config seeded once, optional NFS Hermes Agent Installs Claude Code, the Claude subscription plugin and the plex-fix skill inside the running container

docs.text: Role Purpose common Apt cache update, timezone configuration docker_service Deploy Docker Compose service (create dir, template compose, pull images, start) tailscale Install and configure Tailscale (client or subnet_router mode) nfs_mount Mount NFS shares (used by apps with nfs: true)

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Connection refused — Verify the VM is running and the IP in hosts.ini is correct. Test with ssh sfcal@<ip>.

"No hosts matched" — The host group in the playbook doesn't match any group in hosts.ini, or none of its hosts are in the site group ENV= picks (site_<env>). Check group names match (e.g., infra_networking, app_kosync).

Handler not triggered — Handlers only run when a task reports changed. If you need to force a restart, use --force-handlers or run the service command directly.

Secrets decryption failure — Ensure the Age key is at ~/.config/sops/age/keys.txt and community.sops is installed.

docs.title: Config Reference
docs.text: Consolidated reference for configuration formats used across the homelab.

docs.title: Service Definitions
docs.text:
Service definitions drive both DNS records and reverse proxy entries. They come from two sources:

  1. App registry — apps in the site's registry group_vars/site_<env>/apps.yml declare a proxy: block; registry_services (in group_vars/all/vars.yml) gets an entry for each one (see App Registry)
  2. Manual per-domain files — for services outside the catalog (third-party devices, media stack, monitoring, Frigate, cloud gaming), each domain has its own file in the proxy folder of the site that is primary for it, ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_<env>/proxy/:
site_wil/proxy/
├── 5am.video.yml          # video_services
├── 5am.cloud.yml          # cloud_services
└── wil.5am.cloud.yml      # wil_services
site_ldn/proxy/
└── ldn.5am.cloud.yml      # ldn_services

docs.title: Service Entry Format
docs.text:
- name: myapp              # Subdomain → myapp.wil.5am.cloud
  backend_host: 10.2.20.60
  backend_port: 8080
  proxied: true             # true = Caddy proxy, false = DNS direct

docs.title: All Fields
docs.text:
Field Required Default Description name yes — Subdomain name backend_host yes — Backend IP address backend_port yes — Backend port proxied yes — Route through Caddy (true) or direct DNS (false) enabled no true Set false to disable both DNS and proxy dns no — Set external to skip internal A record tls_skip_verify no false Backend uses self-signed HTTPS forward_headers no false Add X-Real-IP, X-Forwarded-For headers host_header no — Override Host header sent to upstream encode no — Response encoding (e.g., gzip) read_buffer no — Read buffer size auth no false Require a Kanidm login

For registry-generated entries, backend_host is derived (first inventory host of the app's host_group) and backend_port defaults to the app's port — the proxy: block supplies name, domain, proxied, and any optional fields.

docs.title: Service Aggregation
docs.text:
services in group_vars/all/vars.yml combines the site's manual domain lists (injecting the domain name), appends the registry-generated entries, and keeps only the zones of the host's site:

services: >-
  {{
    (
      (video_services | default([]) | map('combine', {'domain': '5am.video'}) | list) +
      (cloud_services | default([]) | map('combine', {'domain': '5am.cloud'}) | list) +
      (wil_services | default([]) | map('combine', {'domain': 'wil.5am.cloud'}) | list) +
      (ext_services | default([]) | map('combine', {'domain': 'ext.5am.cloud'}) | list) +
      (sfc_services | default([]) | map('combine', {'domain': 'sfc.al'}) | list) +
      (ldn_services | default([]) | map('combine', {'domain': 'ldn.5am.cloud'}) | list) +
      registry_services
    ) | selectattr('domain', 'in', sites[site].zones) | list
  }}

Both BIND9 and Caddy templates consume the unified services list.

docs.title: VM Definitions
docs.text: VMs are defined in HCL maps in terraform/environments/<env>/vms.auto.tfvars. See Terraform — VM Module Variables for the full field reference.

docs.title: App Registry
docs.text:
Data-driven apps are defined in the registry of the site that hosts them, ansible/inventory/group_vars/site_<env>/apps.yml — the service catalog for images, ports, and proxy/DNS metadata:

apps:
  myapp:
    host_group: app_myapp      # Ansible inventory group
    # renovate: datasource=docker
    image: "myimage:latest"     # Primary container image
    port: 8080                  # Exposed port; default proxy backend_port
    proxy:                      # Optional — omit for no DNS/proxy entry
      name: myapp               # Subdomain
      domain: wil.5am.cloud
      proxied: true             # Required (no default in zone template)
      # Optional: tls_skip_verify, forward_headers, host_header, encode,
      #           read_buffer, auth, dns, enabled, backend_port (overrides port)
    # Optional:
    # nfs: true                 # Mount NFS shares
    # user: "1000"              # Service user
    # group: "1000"             # Service group

docs.title: Image Keys
docs.text:
There is no images: list — deploy-app.yml derives the pre-pull list from every key ending in image (top level and one nesting level down). Renovate updates these automatically, so image keys must follow these rules:

  • # renovate: datasource=docker comment directly above the image key
  • Key ends in image (e.g., image, db_image, redis_image) with no hyphens in the key
  • Value is double-quoted

docs.title: Multi-Service Apps
docs.text:
Apps that run several containers nest sub-services one level deep, each with its own image, port, and proxy: block (sub-keys must be hyphen-free):

apps:
  work:
    host_group: app_work
    microbin:
      # renovate: datasource=docker
      image: "danielszabo99/microbin:latest"
      port: 8081
      proxy:
        name: bin
        domain: ldn.5am.cloud
        proxied: true
    another_svc:
      # ...

Compose templates read these via apps.work.<svc>.*.

Prefix Purpose Example infra_* Infrastructure services infra_networking, infra_ca app_* Applications app_mediastack, app_kosync site_* Sites; every host is in one site_wil, site_ldn

Parent groups: [infrastructure:children] and [apps:children] aggregate all groups of each type.

docs.title: Global Variables
docs.text:
Defined in ansible/inventory/group_vars/all/vars.yml, filled in from the site's row in all/sites.yml (see Environments):

domains: "{{ sites[site].zones | map('community.general.dict_kv', 'name') | list }}"
system_timezone: "{{ sites[site].tz }}"

docs.title: Filesystem Layout
docs.text:
Hosts follow the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard. The paths are hard-coded in the playbooks and templates; each stack is a project (work, monitoring, media-stack, ...):

Path Holds /opt/<project>/ compose.yaml, Dockerfiles, config rendered by Ansible /var/lib/<project>/<service>/ State the containers write: databases, caches, uploads /var/log/<project>/ Log files mounted out of containers /srv/<project>/ Files served to clients: netboot images, the ROM library

Stacks with their own playbook define <stack>_deploy_path / <stack>_data_path in their group_vars so the tasks and templates share one definition.

docs.title: Packer
docs.text: Packer builds cloud-init-enabled VM templates on Proxmox.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
# Build Ubuntu Server template
task packer:build-ubuntu ENV=wil

# Build Ubuntu Desktop template
task packer:build-ubuntu-desktop ENV=wil

# Build Windows template (needs the Windows and virtio-win ISOs on Proxmox, see below)
task packer:build-windows ENV=ldn

# Clean up logs and ISOs
task packer:clean

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
Template File Description Ubuntu Server ubuntu-server-base.pkr.hcl Ubuntu Server with Docker, Node Exporter, Lazydocker, mDNS (avahi) Ubuntu Desktop ubuntu-desktop-base.pkr.hcl Ubuntu Server install with ubuntu-desktop-minimal on top (GNOME, no browser), KasmVNC, NAS share at /mnt/data, mDNS (avahi); no Docker or Node Exporter Windows windows-base.pkr.hcl Windows 11 (or Server) for one-off VMs: UEFI + TPM 2.0, unattended install, virtio-win guest tools (drivers, QEMU and SPICE agents), Remote Desktop on, console clipboard

Templates produce images named <template>-<env>-base (e.g., ubuntu-server-wil-base).

docs.title: What Templates Include
docs.text:
The Ubuntu Server template (primary) installs:

  1. Cloud-init configuration for Proxmox
  2. Docker and Docker Compose
  3. Lazydocker (terminal UI for Docker)
  4. Node Exporter v1.9.1 (Prometheus metrics)
  5. avahi-daemon (mDNS, IPv4 only) — every clone answers to <hostname>.local; the gateway's mDNS reflector carries that to client VLANs
  6. Cleanup (remove SSH keys, machine ID, apt cache)

docs.title: Ubuntu Desktop Template
docs.text:
Built the same way as the Ubuntu Server template: same ISO, same autoinstall (http/user-data), same mDNS setup. Instead of Docker and Node Exporter the build then installs ubuntu-desktop-minimal, the default selection of the Ubuntu Desktop installer (GNOME, basic utilities), and KasmVNC. It leaves out the Firefox snap, whose downloads took over an hour of the build, so clones have no browser, and the first-login welcome wizard. The prompt to upgrade to the next Ubuntu release is turned off. No separate Desktop ISO is needed.

It is still a cloud-init template, so clone it with the Terraform VM module (template_name = "ubuntu-desktop-<env>-base", memory of 4096 or more, disk_size no smaller than the template's 32G) or by hand from the Proxmox UI. Clones start a GNOME desktop at boot and serve it through KasmVNC.

docs.title: KasmVNC
docs.text:
kasmvnc@<ssh_username>.service runs the desktop on https://<clone>:8444 with a self-signed certificate, the same on every clone. The login is ssh_username / kasmvnc_password from the credentials file. It is not ssh_password because the port is open to the whole network and that user has passwordless sudo.

To put a clone behind SSO, add it to Kasm as a KasmVNC server on port 8444 with that login. Kasm sends the password itself, so the user only sees the SSO login. GNOME's lock screen is off on every clone (files/kasmvnc/90-no-lock-screen.gschema.override), so there is no second login inside the desktop.

The Proxmox console still has the GNOME login screen (ssh_username / ssh_password). GNOME runs one session per user and KasmVNC's is already running, so stop the service before logging in there.

GPU rendering is per VM and not in the template. After mapping a VF to a clone, install linux-generic-hwe-24.04 (the template's 6.8 kernel has no driver for the Arc Pro B50), add the user to group render, set desktop.gpu.hw3d: true in ~/.vnc/kasmvnc.yaml, and reboot.

docs.title: NAS share
docs.text: nfs_share in ubuntu-desktop-variables.pkrvars.hcl is mounted at /mnt/data: the same export and path the nfs_mount role gives WIL's media VM, and LDN clones reach it over the Tailscale tunnel. It mounts on first use and shows in the Files sidebar. A clone that cannot reach the NAS still boots. Files written from a clone end up owned by root on the share, and any user on the clone can write to all of it.

docs.title: Other differences from the server template
docs.text:
Two things differ from the server template on clones:

  • The password keeps working, at the console only. cloud-init normally locks its default user's password on a clone's first boot, which would leave no way to log in at the GNOME screen, so the template sets lock_passwd: false for that user. The same file (/etc/cloud/cloud.cfg.d/99-default-user.cfg) sets ssh_pwauth: false, so SSH takes keys only: Terraform clones get their key as usual, a clone made by hand needs one in its Cloud-Init tab.
  • NetworkManager runs the network instead of systemd-networkd (the desktop packages make it the netplan renderer). It is fed by the same Proxmox cloud-init settings, so ip_address, gateway and nameserver work as usual. The build disables systemd-networkd-wait-online, which would otherwise hold every boot for two minutes waiting for an interface systemd-networkd no longer has.

The build also sets MUTTER_DEBUG_KMS_THREAD_TYPE=user in /etc/environment. Without it GNOME Shell is killed about two seconds after starting on Proxmox's default display whenever its display thread runs with realtime priority, and the login screen restarts six times on every boot before it stays up.

docs.title: Windows Template
docs.text:
For one-off Windows VMs: build the template once, then clone it from the Proxmox UI (right-click → Clone, full clone) or with qm clone <template-vmid> <new-vmid> --name win-test --full 1. Clones boot straight to the login screen, get an address by DHCP (shown on the VM's Summary page via the guest agent) and have Remote Desktop enabled. Log in with ssh_username / ssh_password from the environment and credentials var files. Copy and paste works over Remote Desktop and, via the clipboard panel, in the Proxmox noVNC console.

Before the first build, upload two ISOs to the node's ISO storage (local → ISO Images) and point iso_file / virtio_iso_file in environments/<env>/windows-variables.pkrvars.hcl at them:

ISO Source Windows installer Windows 11 x64 ISO (the link expires, so download in a browser and upload); Windows Server evaluation ISOs work too virtio-win stable-virtio/virtio-win.iso (disk/network drivers, QEMU guest agent)

How the build works: Packer generates a small ISO with the answer file (files/windows/autounattend.xml.pkrtpl) and files/windows/setup.ps1, attaches it next to the two ISOs above and presses a key at "Press any key to boot from CD or DVD". Setup runs unattended (VirtIO drivers from the virtio-win ISO, GPT/UEFI layout, local admin account, OOBE skipped). At the first automatic logon setup.ps1 enables WinRM, installs the virtio-win guest tools (drivers, QEMU guest agent, SPICE agent) and turns the autologon off again; Packer then connects over WinRM, runs a short check and converts the VM to windows-<env>-base. The generated ISO is deleted from Proxmox afterwards. Expect 10–15 minutes.

Packer cannot set the display's clipboard option, so after a build enable it on the template by hand: Hardware → Display → Edit → Advanced → Clipboard: VNC (or qm set <vmid> --vga std,clipboard=vnc on the node). Clones inherit it, and together with the SPICE agent that setup.ps1 installs it gives the noVNC console its clipboard panel.

Secure Boot certificates: on a node with pve-edk2-firmware 4.2025.05-1 or newer, Proxmox fills a new EFI disk with both the 2011 and the 2023 Microsoft UEFI certificates and marks it ms-cert=2023k in the VM config (visible in qm config <vmid>), so a fresh build and its clones are correct from the start. The Packer Proxmox plugin (1.2.3) has no option for this and needs none. A template built before that firmware version, and every clone of it, lacks the marker and the node warns at VM start that the 2011 certificates expired in June 2026. Rebuild such a template, and fix an existing clone while it is shut down with qm enroll-efi-keys <vmid> (UI: Hardware → EFI Disk → Disk Action → Enroll Updated Certificates); if BitLocker protectors are active in the guest, suspend them first or Windows asks for the recovery key.

Things to know:

  • windows_image_name selects the edition inside the ISO (Windows 11 Pro by default; Windows 11 Enterprise Evaluation, Windows Server 2025 SERVERSTANDARD, …). Set virtio_driver_os to the matching driver folder (w11, 2k25, …) and windows_language to the ISO's language.
  • No sysprep: clones share hostname and SID. Fine for throwaway instances; the template is not meant for domain joins.
  • No cloud-init: Windows ignores the Proxmox cloud-init drive, so clones are not managed by the Terraform VM module (which is cloud-init shaped). Clone by hand.
  • setup.ps1 leaves its logs at C:\Windows\Temp\packer-setup.log and C:\Windows\Temp\virtio-win-guest-tools.log on the template.
  • NAS share: set smb_server, smb_share and smb_username in windows-variables.pkrvars.hcl and smb_password in the credentials file, and every clone has \\<server>\<share> as a persistent Z: drive for the local administrator. smb-share.ps1 stores the login in Credential Manager and runs net use /persistent:yes, so Windows reconnects the drive at logon on its own (SMB rather than NFS: no UID/GID mapping, no extra client). The NAS must be reachable from the build VM. Leave smb_server empty for no share.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
Proxmox API credentials (and, for the Windows template, the ssh_password of the local administrator and the optional smb_password NAS password) are stored in SOPS-encrypted files:

# Edit credentials
sops packer/environments/wil/credentials.wil.pkrvars.hcl.sops

A build decrypts the file for the one packer build command (sops exec-file), so no plain-text credentials.<env>.pkrvars.hcl is needed.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
401 Unauthorized — The Proxmox API token is invalid or lacks permissions. Verify the token in credentials.<env>.pkrvars.hcl.sops (open it with sops). The token needs VM.Allocate, VM.Clone, Datastore.AllocateSpace, and related permissions.

Template name conflict — A template with the same name already exists. Delete the old template from Proxmox first: qm destroy <vmid>.

ISO not found — The iso_file path must match an ISO uploaded to Proxmox storage. Check with pvesm list <storage> on the Proxmox host.

Build hangs at SSH — The VM can't reach the internet for package installation, or cloud-init hasn't configured networking. Check Proxmox network bridge and VLAN settings.

Windows build never connects over WinRM — Open the VM console in Proxmox. If it still shows the firmware or a boot menu, the "Press any key" prompt was missed: raise boot_wait or the number of <spacebar> presses in windows-base.pkr.hcl. If Setup is asking for a product key, set windows_product_key to the generic key for the edition. If Setup says it cannot find a disk, virtio_driver_os does not match the Windows version (folders on the virtio-win ISO). If Windows is at the desktop, read C:\Windows\Temp\packer-setup.log for the failing step in setup.ps1.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
"task: Task not found" — Check the exact task name with task --list-all. Namespace and command are separated by :.

"Pass ENV=" — ENV has no default. A task that needs it stops before it runs anything when ENV is missing; add ENV=wil, ENV=ldn or ENV=ovh.

Ansible timeout — Add -vvv for verbose output: edit the task in .taskfiles/ansible/Taskfile.yaml and add -vvv to EXTRA_ARGS.

docs.title: Terraform
docs.text: Terraform provisions VMs on Proxmox by cloning Packer-built templates.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
# Deploy all VMs
task terraform:deploy ENV=wil

# Deploy a single VM
task terraform:deploy-vm ENV=wil VM=networking

# Destroy a single VM
task terraform:destroy-vm ENV=wil VM=networking

# Clean up state files
task terraform:clean ENV=wil

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
VMs are defined as a map in terraform/environments/<env>/vms.auto.tfvars. The root module iterates over this map with for_each and calls the VM module for each entry.

terraform/
├── main.tf                          # Root module (for_each over vms)
├── modules/vm/
│   ├── main.tf                      # proxmox_virtual_environment_vm resource (bpg/proxmox)
│   └── variables.tf                 # VM variable definitions
└── environments/
    ├── wil/
    │   ├── main.tf                  # Calls root module
    │   ├── variables.tf             # Variable declarations
    │   ├── providers.tf             # Proxmox provider config
    │   ├── vms.auto.tfvars          # VM definitions
    │   └── terraform.tfstate        # State file
    └── ldn/

docs.title: VM Definition Format
docs.text:

    vmid           = 1000

    cores          = 2

docs.title: Implementation Details
docs.text:
• Provider — bpg/proxmox, pinned in versions.tf. It takes the endpoint and API token from the variables in the site's terraform.tfvars.sops (proxmox_api_url without /api2/json, <token id>=<secret>), which each task decrypts for its one command (sops exec-file).
  • Full clones — VMs are full clones, not linked. Independent of templates after creation. The template is looked up by name on every plan, so a missing or duplicated template name fails the plan (it never destroys anything).
  • Cloud-init — Static IP via the initialization block (ipconfig0: ip=<address>/24,gw=<gateway>, drive on ide0). Assumes /24 subnets. bpg keeps cloud-init values of the template that the module does not set, such as a cipassword set by hand on the template; telmate removed them. The login keys (ssh_public_key in terraform.tfvars.sops) are written when a VM is created and ignored afterwards: add a key to a running VM in its authorized_keys.
  • State — Per-environment state files at terraform/environments/<env>/terraform.tfstate (not in git). Both sites have one. To import a VM made outside Terraform, see Proxmox — Terraform notes.
  • QEMU agent — Enabled on all VMs (installed in Packer templates).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Plan error at clone.vm_id — "Attempt to get attribute from null value" means no template named template_name exists on proxmox_node; "must be a list, set, or tuple value with either zero or one elements" means two templates share the name. Check with qm list on the Proxmox host. Names follow ubuntu-server-<env>-base.

"VMID already exists" — Another VM uses that ID. Check qm list or the existing entries in vms.auto.tfvars.

State out of sync — If a VM was deleted outside Terraform, it is still in the state. Drop it with terraform state rm 'module.infrastructure.module.vms["<key>"]' in terraform/environments/<env>/ and redeploy. (task terraform:clean only removes the plugin cache.)

Provider authentication error — Verify the Proxmox API credentials in the encrypted terraform.tfvars.sops. Open it with sops terraform/environments/<env>/terraform.tfvars.sops. The tasks decrypt it themselves and pass it with -var-file, which wins over a plain-text terraform.tfvars left in the folder, so that copy is no longer needed.
